#305. The world has a new plan to save nature, but it still needs the money

A new action plan aims to rescue 2030 nature targets as financing remains inadequate.

The world is set to miss its 2030 conservation goals as finance and action have fallen short, leaders recognized at a UN biodiversity summit in Armenia’s capital, where they agreed to step up efforts after a final overnight session.

Representatives from almost 200 countries gathered in Yerevan over the past two weeks to review progress on a landmark agreement set four years ago to protect about a third of the world’s land and seas by 2030.

The COP17 talks on biodiversity concluded on Saturday with a recognition that conservation efforts were so far too slow to realistically achieve the goals of the 2022 Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.

A plan was agreed to accelerate progress ahead of the next summit in Ecuador in two years, dubbed the Yerevan Pathway. It would mean redoubling efforts to tackle subsidies and incentives that are harmful to nature, increasing financial, scientific, and technical support for developing countries, and strengthening monitoring and reporting mechanisms.

Steven Guilbeault, former Canadian minister of environment and climate change, said that finance remained one of the biggest obstacles to achieving global biodiversity goals.

The fact that a fund agreed at the last meeting—for companies profiting from genetic materials to voluntarily contribute to—stood largely empty was “especially disappointing.”

“We need to mobilize substantially more public and private finance, reform subsidies that harm nature, and ensure that funding reaches the countries and communities on the front lines of the nature crisis,” he said.

Catherine Weller, global policy director at the campaign group Fauna & Flora, said the Yerevan agreement was welcome but also noted that funding fell far short of a pledge that had been a key part of the 2022 deal. “In a world of trillionaires, we can certainly afford to spend $200 billion a year on protecting and restoring the very thing keeping us all alive: nature,” she said.

Conference organizers said governments, philanthropists, and businesses had announced close to $2 billion in new financial commitments to coincide with the Armenian gathering.

This included a commitment by the Netherlands to contribute $500 million to the Tropical Forest Forever Facility, a Brazilian initiative to pay countries to keep their forests standing. The pledge was announced in the Dutch parliament the day after Brazilian leader Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva was re-elected as president, to the relief of many attending the biodiversity summit.

After the close of the conference, Carina Pimenta, Brazil’s national secretary for bioeconomy, highlighted Lula’s record of protecting the Amazon rainforest and spoke of hope. “At a time of growing global uncertainty, the Yerevan Declaration sends a powerful message: world leaders recognize that protecting biodiversity is essential to food security, livelihoods, and economic resilience,” she said.

A growing number of countries to have drawn up national diversity plans, and the new pledge to the Brazilian fund, were “reasons for cautious optimism,” said Brian O’Donnell, director at Campaign for Nature.

But international funding for protected and conserved areas has fallen in a number of countries over years of disruption from war and high energy prices, with a 27 percent decline in environmental funding for the 2026-30 period.

#302. Google's Ocarina of Time Easter egg is a link to a past when Search wasn't horrible

Turn the clock back to 1998 ahead of Nintendo's remake of the classic Zelda game.

Nintendo's remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is out this week and Google Search is marking the occasion with an appropriate Easter egg. If you search for "Zelda" or "Ocarina of Time," you'll see an animation of the Master Sword pop up in the corner. Click or tap on this and a loading screen of sorts that features a Triforce will take over the tab for a moment.

After that animation clears, the search results will look like they're from 1998, the year that the original version of Ocarina of Time debuted on the Nintendo 64. You'll see blue hyperlinks to relevant webpages and brief excerpts from them, listed in order of apparent relevance, which is how a search engine is supposed to work. The classic "I'm Feeling Lucky" button that takes you to a random page is there too.

Unfortunately, this Easter egg only seems to work for searches related to the game. Looking up something else takes you back to the current, far worse Search results page. This is an Easter egg that's supposed to invoke nostalgia, though it's doing that in a way that Google perhaps didn't intend.

All it's really doing is reminding me of a time before Google made Search so much worse, from packing the results with ads to eventually foisting AI Mode and AI Overviews upon everyone. (Google said last week AI Mode is having an impact on how much it makes from ads in traditional Search. Its solution to eating its own lunch? More ads in AI Mode.)

There is a way to have more of a traditional Search experience on Google if you'd prefer not to decamp to an alternative search engine. If you click on the Web tab on a Google Search results page, you'll see actual webpages that are relevant to your query with none of the AI Overview cruft. You can set things up in your browser so that this is your default Google experience as well. The aptly named TenBlueLinks has easy-to-follow guides on how to do that.

#301. These are the animals people most want to see photographed

Editor’s Note:  Call to Earth is a CNN editorial series committed to reporting on the environmental challenges facing our planet, together with the solutions. Rolex’s Perpetual Planet initiative has partnered with CNN to drive awareness and education around key sustainability issues and to inspire positive action.

Originally a term used by trophy hunters in Africa, the “Big Five” described the animals most challenging to shoot and kill: the lion, elephant, leopard, rhino, and buffalo. Nowadays, it is more loosely used to refer to some of Africa’s largest and most iconic animals.

However, British photographer Graeme Green has reclaimed the narrative, creating a global “New Big Five” for wildlife photography. In 2021, 50,000 people around the world voted for the five animals they would most like to photograph, or see photographed, in the wild. Five animals were crowned the winners: the elephant, polar bear, lion, gorilla and tiger.

This week, sees the publication of “The New Big 5” photography book, which features images of those animals and other at-risk wildlife, from photography legends such as Ami Vitale, Steve McCurry and Paul Nicklen, and essays from famous conservationists and activists including like Jane Goodall and Paula Kahumbu.

Green says that the book celebrates wildlife and is a global call to action on issues impacting wildlife, including habitat loss, poaching, pollution and climate change.

Green was on assignment in Botswana at least a decade ago when he came up with the idea for a project to encourage people to “shoot with a camera, not a gun,” he says.

“I thought this would be a way to get people really focusing on wildlife, thinking about the wildlife they love, thinking about the animals that are at risk.”

Ten photographs that made the world wake up to climate change

In total, the book includes the work of 144 globally renowned wildlife photographers from Ecuador to India. Curating the images took nearly two years of work, says Green.

“I think these are some of the most beautiful and creative images that I’ve seen put together in one book,” says Green. “These are the species that we are at risk of losing.”

According to the UN, nature is declining at an unprecedented rate, with around one million of the planet’s animal and plant species facing extinction. The “New Big 5,” all of which are threatened, act as ambassadors for what is happening in the natural world, says Green.

As well as being a powerful reminder of what we stand to lose, the book also points people towards potential solutions. Featured essays explore the benefits of rewilding and the importance of indigenous communities in conservation.

A chapter on endangered species from bees to blue whales illustrates the alarming threat climate change poses to animals outside of the “New Big 5.” “That’s only the tip of the iceberg – I could have included thousands of pictures because that’s how serious the situation is,” says Green.

Why a wildlife photographer took 40,000 photos to capture these extraordinary birds

Jane Goodall, a leading conservationist who also wrote the afterword to the book, said in a press release that “we have a window of time during which we can start to heal some of the harm we have inflicted on the natural world, but only if we get together and take action now.

“I hope the photos will lead people into the wonderful worlds of these iconic species. Then, perhaps, other people will become involved in helping to create a world where wildlife can flourish for future generations to enjoy,” she said.

“The New Big 5: A Global Photography Project For Endangered Wildlife,” by Graeme Green, published by Earth Aware Editions, is on sale from April 4, 2023.

This story has been updated to reflect the range of issues covered by the book.

#299. Nagoshi Studio, from the creator of the Yakuza series, officially shuts down

It’s unclear what will happen to the studio’s work on Gang of Dragon.

Less than a year after the announcement of its first game Gang of Dragon, Nagoshi Studio has officially closed its doors. The studio, which was founded by Toshihiro Nagoshi of Yakuza franchise fame, announced its conclusion in the Japan government's official gazette Kanpo, stating the company was dissolved on October 31 during a shareholders meeting.

After the success of the Yakuza series, Nagoshi went on to create Nagoshi Studio and began work on Gang of Dragon, releasing the game's first trailer in December 2025. The upcoming game looked to be an evolution of the franchise that still covered the organized crime scene in Tokyo's Kabuchiko district through the lens of the new protagonist, Shin Ji-Seong, but potentially with a more serious tone. Despite the hype from the trailer, one of the game's backers, NetEase, decided to pull funding from the studio, according to a Bloomberg report. The game reportedly still needed more than $44 million to reach the finish line, so Nagoshi Studio was looking for financial support elsewhere to complete the game.

However, now that the company has official shut down, Nagoshi Studio will start liquidating its assets and sorting out liabilities, according to its notice published in Kanpo. The game's Steam store page is still live, but it's unlikely that Gang of Dragon will make it out of development limbo anytime soon.

#296. F1 in Mexico City: Yet another Ferrari fiasco, but that’s not all

There was plenty of drama on and off the track for Formula 1 this weekend.

Formula 1 has a new World Drivers’ Champion. Just a few months after turning 20, Kimi Antonelli sealed his first title this weekend at Mexico City, becoming the sport’s youngest-ever champion. Elsewhere, there was drama aplenty, perhaps a consequence of the thin air affecting decision-making in some cases. The race was Ferrari’s to win, but yet again, the team handed victory to a rival this season, in this case Red Bull. Further down the grid, we saw a last-minute driver change in the Haas team, synchronized retirements from both Aston Martins, and the wheels literally coming off Cadillac Racing. And there was I, expecting a dull weekend.

It might not be as high as Pikes Peak, but at an elevation of 7,350 feet (2,240 m) above sea level, the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez provides a unique challenge on the F1 calendar. Wings that would create huge amounts of downforce at circuits like Monaco just generate Monza-like levels in Mexico, and there’s little slipstream effect when following another car.

Cooling tends to be a problem, too, with insufficient airflow across radiators, and obviously engine power is reduced with less oxygen to burn. The track is very flat, with a rather low-grip surface and mostly medium- and slow-speed corners, including a processional route through a stadium that was built in the 1990s, plus a very long run from the start into turn 1.

Friday’s first practice saw 10 rookie drivers substitute in for series regulars—each team must run a young or test driver in each of their two cars at least twice in a season. Make that six times in the case of Cadillac?

The American startup team wants IndyCar star Colton Herta to race in F1, but Herta needs a total of 40 points over three years to get the requisite F1 super license. Sadly, his IndyCar record was too inconsistent—10th place in 2023, 2nd in 2024, but then 7th again in 2025—so he entered F2 this year, both to learn the circuits and to finish well enough in that championship to earn the remaining points.

That hasn’t happened, but you also earn a point for completing 100 km in an FP1 session, and Herta stepped into the Cadillac in Barcelona, Italy, Hungary, and in Texas. His run in Italy was cut short by unreliability, so Cadillac put him in the car again this weekend, hoping it would be the final run.

But it turns out they hadn’t added the numbers properly. Rather than pulling Herta’s IndyCar results from the official scoring, the team apparently relied on IndyCar’s erroneous website. Instead of starting the year with 36 super license points, Herta only had 35, and with four successful FP1 runs under his belt, he still needs one more point if the team wants to replace an underperforming Valteri Bottas next year, something that should happen with another run next time out in Brazil.

It’s not the first time that paperwork has proved to be a problem for the American team, which almost lost a chance to enter the sport after FIA emails went to its spam folder in 2024.

Friday’s second practice session also had more action than normal. Max Verstappen and Liam Lawson both sat out FP1 so rookies could drive their cars, which may have contributed to both being too eager to set a fast time in FP2. As Lawson’s Racing Bull got held up by Carlos Sainz’ slow Williams in front, Verstappen wanted past in the Red Bull, but both drivers were intransigent, and neither was prepared to yield. Paint was traded and cars were damaged, and both drivers were handed a one-place grid penalty for failing to behave themselves.

FP2 also probably marked the end of Esteban Ocon’s F1 career, at least for now. The French driver was upset with his team about their choice of tires for his long run, which evidently escalated once he was out of the car. On Saturday, Ocon had been benched and replaced with Ryo Hirakawa, Haas’ reserve driver and two-time World Endurance Champion with Toyota. Haas had already announced that Ocon was not rejoining the team in 2027, opting instead for F1 driver Rafael Camara, who will probably race for the team in Brazil, as Hirakawa will be racing his Toyota that weekend.

For most of this year, Ferrari has had a particular form. The team often tops the practice times on Friday but then fails to follow up on Saturday, often in the final qualifying session. That didn’t happen in Mexico, and Lewis Hamilton was able to claim his first pole position for Ferrari and his 105th in the sport. George Russell’s Mercedes qualified second, followed by Charles Leclerc’s Ferrari. Verstappen should have been fourth, but that Friday clash saw Antonelli moved into that spot. As it happens, the grid demotion put Verstappen on the clean side of the track, which he used to his advantage.

Both Ferraris got off the line well, as did Verstappen and Antonelli. Russell’s hybrid system derated halfway down the straight, ruining his race well before the first corner. With Hamilton in the lead and Leclerc in second place, the plan should have been obvious: settle into a 1-2 and win the race. Unfortunately, the idea of supporting his teammate is utterly alien to Leclerc, who showed us why he has 27 pole positions but only nine wins in eight years. Once more this year, the Ferraris raced each other as if a championship were at stake, and once more they snatched defeat from the jaws of victory.

Going into turn 4, both drivers went off track and rejoined. The race stewards had been extremely clear that leaving the track and gaining a permanent advantage at turns 1 or 4 on the first lap would result in a penalty unless the driver gave the place back. Hamilton did not gain a lasting advantage, but Leclerc did, staying in clean air up front and building enough of a lead that the paltry five-second penalty that was eventually handed down kept him ahead of Hamilton after their stops.

But it didn’t keep him ahead of Verstappen, who stopped at the same time as Leclerc but emerged in the lead, a lead he would keep until the end.

It wasn’t an easy drive to the checkered flag, however. We’re accustomed to Lance Stroll’s Aston Martin breaking down on track and triggering a safety car or a virtual safety car, and this race was no exception. It happened early, on lap 7, while the other Aston Martin, driven by Fernando Alonso, retired to its garage.

Cadillac has also had plenty of reliability problems this year, usually with its front brakes overheating. It was even more serious in Mexico: On lap 44, Bottas’ front left suspension failed as he approached turn 1. The heavy crash forced a red flag to repair the barrier, bringing the race to a halt and necessitating a second standing start.

Verstappen kept the lead, demonstrating the superior power output of the Red Bull power unit, even at altitude, over Ferrari’s. A furious Hamilton passed Leclerc, who compounded his original error by badly locking his front tires, wearing a flat spot down to the cord. The safety car came out again on lap 59, when Arvid Lindblad’s Racing Bull was taken out by McLaren’s Oscar Piastri.

Up front, Hamilton followed Verstappen by a few tenths of a second but without ever having the speed to try an overtake. The Ferrari might not have had the legs to get past the Red Bull, but its tolerance for riding the curbs, plus the small turbo’s punch out of low-speed corners, was sufficient to give it the edge over 2025 champion Lando Norris’ McLaren, which finished in fifth behind Leclerc.

After the race, Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur said, “I always expect everyone to show respect for the brand, the team, our partners and, above all, the 2,000 people working for us back home. They put an incredible amount of effort into what we do, working day and night at the factory to improve the car and bring upgrades to the track. That’s why missing out on a win in this way is difficult to accept.”

“The core thing to remember, which maybe comes with age, is that every decision you make in the car impacts all the people that work in the background for the whole team,” said a frustrated Hamilton after the race. “A part of our contract is we have to work as a team, which we could have easily done today. So it’s a shame to see us lose as we did. And that will continue unless action is taken, and a real deep, serious conversation is had, so it shouldn’t happen moving forward.”

Hamilton pointed to Leclerc’s “do-or-die, either I win or none of us do” attitude as a problem, ruing the loss of what could have been the team’s best result all year. “It was just unnecessary,” he said. “I think we could have easily had that 1-2, which would have been huge for the team and for everyone back at the factory who’s worked so hard to bring us these upgrades.”

Other teams have laid down clear rules to determine the way teammates race each other—at Mercedes, Toto Wolff began making Hamilton and Nico Rosberg pay for any damage they caused to the cars if they came together on track, and McLaren had its famous Papaya rules. At Ferrari, both drivers are free to race each other, and both are jockeying to be seen as team leader for next year. Now Vasseur has to try to get both Hamilton and Leclerc under control, because if Ferrari keeps giving away race wins like this, his position has to be increasingly untenable.

#295. What to do if your smart home devices keep disconnecting from Wi-Fi

It's strange that Apple is only now beginning to take the smart home market seriously with the launch of the HomeView smart display and the rest of the Apple Home Collection. Affordable consumer gear has been around for years, and when it's well-made and well-configured, it can not only simplify your life but also save you money. Smart thermostats are more efficient, and smart lighting can be set to turn on only when and where you need it — although it's more fun to make your living room look like Los Angeles in Blade Runner 2049.

One hassle is that some accessories don't play well with Wi-Fi. They have a tendency to drop out of apps, assuming you can even set them up in the first place. And needless to say, a home fixture you can't count on is all but worthless. You wouldn't put up with a microwave that only cooked dinner on Tuesdays and Fridays.

Thankfully, there are a few tactics you can use to cope with these misbehaving devices. We're not going to lie, though — in some circumstances, a hardware upgrade is in order. You may want to minimize the number of Wi-Fi-based products in your home in general.

If you're still using a Wi-Fi 5 router, stop everything and upgrade to Wi-Fi 6 or 7. The issue is connection limits. On Wi-Fi 5, the practical limit for simultaneous connections is around 10 to 25 devices, perhaps 30 if you're lucky. That's plenty in a home without smart home gear, but once accessories start filling up those connection slots, problems are inevitable. Your router is going to start kicking some devices to make room, and chances are your phone and laptop are going to win out over a lamp.

Another problem is that many cheaper accessories are limited to the 2.4GHz band. On a mesh Wi-Fi system, setting up these accessories can be difficult or impossible, since there's a unified SSID (network ID) with automatic band steering — your phone might end up on 5 or 6GHz, preventing some apps from detecting the new gear. If you're lucky enough to successfully configure a product, there might still be a possibility of later detection failures.

Speaking of which, let's talk about HomeKit. Apple's platform is prone to "No Response" errors in situations where Amazon Alexa and Google Home operate just fine. The company has tried to smooth this out in recent years with an overhauled framework, but if you want a bulletproof setup, you may need an equally bulletproof Wi-Fi network. That could include two or more Apple home hubs for the sake of control redundancy. You can use a mix of HomePods, HomeViews or Apple TV 4Ks.

There's also a more basic concern we haven't touched on yet, and that's range. If an accessory is sitting on the fringes, it's naturally going to drop out when conditions are less than ideal. If you can't reposition devices or your router, it may be time to upgrade to a mesh system, as long as that doesn't wreak havoc for specific accessories. Alternatively, if you have a standalone router, you might try enabling separate 2.4 and 5GHz SSIDs, and forcing all of your smart home accessories over to the longer-range 2.4GHz band.

Ultimately, the best approach is to transition as many accessories as possible over to alternate protocols, namely Thread, Zigbee or Z-Wave. These do require a Wi-Fi hub, or in the case of Thread, a Wi-Fi-enabled "border router" accessory. The benefit, however, is that they not only reduce the burden on your Wi-Fi network but they also tend to be faster and more reliable. They're mesh-based — extending their reach — and hub-based accessories (like Philips Hue Zigbee lights) can continue to run some automations when the internet is down.

Thread is probably your best bet, since some routers, speakers and displays have border router features built in, as do products like Nanoleaf light panels. There is an asterisk, though: bandwidth. Like Zigbee and Z-Wave, Thread is a low-power standard, so it simply can't carry enough data for functions like audio, video or even vacuuming. It's mostly limited to bulbs, locks, plugs and sensors.

Some degree of Wi-Fi reliance is unavoidable, then. But if you find the right mix and know how to troubleshoot recurring issues, it shouldn't be a big deal. Just have fallbacks ready for internet outages.

#294. Giving Marjorie Taylor Greene a platform isn't good for America

Editor’s Note:  Dean Obeidallah, a former attorney, is the host of SiriusXM radio’s daily program “The Dean Obeidallah Show.” Follow him @DeanObeidallah@masto.ai. The opinions expressed in this commentary are his own. View more opinion on CNN.

Last year, GOP Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia spoke at a white nationalist event organized by Holocaust denier Nick Fuentes that caused Republican leaders to denounce her.

Last week, Greene’s Twitter account was temporarily suspended by the Elon Musk-headed platform over a tweet with a graphic referring to a “Trans Day of Vengeance,” as she denounced a planned transgender rights rally.

And come Tuesday, Greene has announced plans to protest in New York City when former President Donald Trump is expected to be arraigned on an indictment of more than 30 counts, calling the proceedings against him an “unconstitutional WITCH HUNT!”

But on Sunday, Greene was featured on CBS’ “60 Minutes” in an interview the long-running show promoted on Twitter with the tease: “Republican Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, nicknamed MTG, isn’t afraid to share her opinions, no matter how intense and in-your-face they are. She sits down with Lesley Stahl this Sunday on 60 Minutes.” The images attached to this tweet by “60 Minutes” include Greene and Stahl walking through the US Capitol, taking a stroll outside and Greene showing Stahl something on her phone.

It's time for Marjorie Taylor Greene to go

In the segment that aired Sunday night, Stahl noted the congresswoman had moved from the fringe to the GOP’s front row in two years despite a “sharp tongue” and “some pretty radical views” as well as “over the top” comments such as “the Democrats are a party of pedophiles.” Stahl also referred to video of Greene chasing a Parkland, Florida, school shooting survivor, still maintaining that the 2020 election was stolen and failing to criticize Trump over spending. (The interview was conducted before news of his indictment.)

But Stahl didn’t mention Greene spoke at a white nationalist event a year ago while a member of Congress or her extreme anti-Muslim views and her defense of January 6 rioters.

Criticism of CBS for amplifying Greene has been swift and well-deserved even before the program aired. Former GOP Rep. Adam Kinzinger of Illinois tweeted beforehand: “Wow. Insane that 60 min would do this.” (Kinzinger is a CNN senior political commentator.)

Journalist Molly Jong-Fast also slammed “60 Minutes” with the tweet: “Attention is currency and 60 minutes is spending its currency on the Jewish space lasers woman.” (Jong-Fast was apparently referring to Greene’s past claim that a massive California wildfire was started by “a laser” beamed from space controlled by a prominent Jewish banking family.)

David Hogg, who survived the 2018 horrific school shooting at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland and has since become an activist against gun violence, responded, “I look forward to your questions about why she thinks school shootings are fake and why she’s supported QAnon.”

Greene amplified the conspiracy theory — two years before being elected to Congress — that the Parkland shooting that took 17 lives was staged. And in 2019, Greene appeared on video confronting Hogg outside the Capitol when he was championing laws to save lives from gun violence, screaming that the then-teenager was a “coward.” She also called Hogg “#littleHitler” on social media.

Greene’s own tweet promoting Sunday’s segment was not filled with her typical smears of “fake news” when she doesn’t like the coverage. Rather, Greene urged people to tune in as she praised “60 Minutes” host Stahl (and misspelled her first name): “It was an honor to spend a few days with the legendary icon Leslie Stahl and talented crew @60Minutes.” Greene added, “Leslie is a trailblazer for women in journalism. And while we may disagree on some issues, I respect her greatly.”

Now, it is true that “60 Minutes” over its 50-plus-year history has featured what the show has dubbed “controversial” guests. These include a 2000 interview with Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh, whose 1995 terrorist attack left 168 dead, including 19 children. And the show did a 1979 interview with Iran’s Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini.

Perhaps “60 Minutes” views Greene — who has repeatedly downplayed and even defended the January 6, 2021, attack plus called for the GOP to become the party of “Christian nationalism” — in the vein of its long list of controversial guests. (CBS had not responded to a request from CNN for comment at time of publishing.)

However, the choice of Greene as a guest instantly recalls the comments of then-CBS CEO Les Moonves during Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign when he admitted that Trump’s candidacy “may not be good for America, but it’s damn good for CBS.” Moonves added, “The money’s rolling in and this is fun. … (T)his is going to be a very good year for us,” concluding, “Sorry. It’s a terrible thing to say. But bring it on, Donald. Keep going.”

Moonves may be gone from CBS, but it appears his mindset continues at “60 Minutes.” And that may be good for “60 Minutes,” but it’s definitely not good for America.

#293. Merz says next German president 'must be a woman' — report

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier's second term is due to end in March next year. Meanwhile, Merz has called for 'digital sovereignty' in the era of AI.

This blog is now closed. It was a round-up of some of the top headlines from and about Germany on November 2, 2026:

We're closing the blog today. Thank you for reading, we'll be back tomorrow again!

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has spoken out in favor of having a woman succeed Frank-Walter Steinmeier as Germany's president.

"I will propose a consensus candidate to the party, a candidate from the political center," Merz said at a non-public meeting of local Christian Democratic Union (CDU) chairs in Berlin, participants told the German DPA news agency.

"I am firm in my belief that it must be a woman," he reportedly added.

Germany's federal president is the country's official head of state, as opposed to the chancellor, who is the head of the government.

Current incumbent Steinmeier, a former Social Democrat (SPD) foreign minister, became president in 2017 and his second term will end in March 2027.

Bavarian premier Markus Söder recently proposed Ilse Aigner from his Christian Social Union (CSU), the CDU's Bavarian sister party.

But the CDU itself may propose an alternative candidate from within its own ranks, with current parliamentary speaker Julia Klöckner, Families Minister Karin Prien and former CDU leader and Defense Minister Annegret Kramp-Karrenbauer all having been mentioned.

The CDU's top leadership is expected to propose a candidate on November 9.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz says Germany must speed up its development of artificial intelligence capabilities to protect its "digital sovereignty" in an era of rapid change.

Speaking at a conference on AI in Berlin, the chancellor said countries risked surrendering control to outside providers by failing to keep pace.

"That is why we must, at all costs, avoid becoming entirely dependent on third parties when it comes to developing and using this ​technology," he said. "And that is why the issue of digital sovereignty in the context of ​AI becomes a truly existential question."

Merz stressed that people and their dignity must remain central to political efforts to manage rapid technological progress, saying AI development should be guided by human values.

He also said adapting to AI-driven changes required "an enormous technological and organizational effort, a far-reaching modernization of our state and our economy."

Merz pointed to Germany's strength as a business location and home of industrial engineering. He also said international cooperation was crucial, and that Berlin would seek to work with like-minded partners such as France and Canada to share knowledge and diversify supply chains.

Merz appointed a minister for digitalization and modernization last year after taking office. Although many German companies have adopted and integrated AI technology, critics say Germany has been too slow to build the digital infrastructure and ​skills needed to exploit it fully.

Alexander Zverev officially rose to the No. 1 spot in the men's tennis rankings on Monday, becoming only the second German man to hold the title after Boris Becker 35 years ago.

"Today is a historic day for German tennis," said German Tennis Federation President Dietloff von Arnim. "Sascha has earned this spot at the top of the world rankings through extraordinary perseverance and hard work."

The 29-year-old beat Flavio Cobolli to win the French Open title in June, before going on to lift the US Open trophy after defeating Ben Shelton in September.

He also reached the final at Wimbledon this year, ultimately falling to Jannik Sinner, and the Australian Open semifinals.

He is the 30th male player to reach No. 1, and the oldest in more than 50 years to top the rankings for the first time.

"I had to wait," said Zverev, who reached the top spot more than four years after becoming No. 2. "But sometimes you've got to wait for the best things in life. I'm super happy, super thrilled."

Sinner, who had been holding the No.1 spot since April 13, dropped to second, ahead of Carlos Alcaraz.

The AfD's foreign policy spokesman, Markus Frohnmaier, said the meeting is likely to take place in Abu Dhabi in early 2027 and will focus on restoring Russian gas deliveries to Germany.

DW understands that AfD leaders Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla would attend the meeting if US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were also present.

Such a meeting would represent a major PR coup for the far-right party, which remains shunned by most of Germany's political establishment despite leading national opinion polls.

"The focus here will be on discussions with the American side, as well as the Russian side, particularly with regard to economic partnership, energy partnership and also the Nord Stream question," Frohnmaier told journalists in Berlin.

According to Frohnmaier, Kirill Dmitriev, a special adviser to Russian President Vladimir Putin, is coordinating with contacts in the US administration.

Dmitriev greeted Witkoff, US President Donald Trump's Middle East envoy, when he arrived in Russia for talks last month.

Dmitriev has also been cultivating contacts in Germany. He and Frohnmaier met at an economic forum in St. Petersburg earlier this year.

While the Abu Dhabi summit is expected to focus on business and economic ties, Frohnmaier said such formats can "establish a framework for dialogue" and help "work toward peace."

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier attended the opening of a new Jewish Academy in Frankfurt on Monday.

The €40-million ($45-million) educational institution, which was inaugurated under tight security, is to be a "place of dialogue," Steinmeier said.

He denounced antisemitism and said it must be "put in its place, without loopholes or reservations," whether it comes from the left or the right of the political spectrum.

The president also warned against what he described as the increasing political exploitation of hatred toward Jews.

The German Retail Association says society as a whole has a responsibility to prevent the kind of violence that followed youth protests in several German cities on Saturday.

In Frankfurt, rioters threw stones and petrol bombs, smashed shop windows and looted businesses. Violent confrontations were also reported in other parts of the country.

"We must not tolerate a social climate in which retailers cannot always be certain, wherever they are, that they can go about their business unhindered," association boss Stefan Genth said.

"This applies to society as a whole. We are all called upon to act," he said, adding that it must be clear that violence, or the threat of it, has no place in Germany.

Tens of thousands of young people demonstrated across the country over the weekend calling for better education funding and measures to bring down the cost of living. The protests were largely peaceful, although in some cities they were followed by rioting and looting.

Genth said it was alarming "that some retailers in certain locations felt compelled last Saturday to take extra security measures or, in some cases, to close their shops entirely."

Chancellor Friedrich Merz is to tell a conference of local party leaders of  his conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) that he saw a positive aspect to weekend youth protests, while condemning violence that occurred in their aftermath.

"I take above all a positive message from the weekend: The young generation is politically engaged and is concerned about its future," he is to say, according to a speech released beforehand to news agencies.

In the planned speech, Merz says the government is making efforts not to burden the younger generation with the costs of an aging society.

"That is why we are carrying out pension reform for young people, why we are concerned about our security, and why we are preparing our economy for the digital future," Merz's speech runs.

However, the chancellor has harsh words for those who rioted and attacked police on the sidelines of the mostly peaceful protests.

"Violence has no place on our streets, and my government will show no tolerance in this regard," the speech says.

"Anyone who attacks police officers and emergency service personnel and loots shops is attacking our freedom, mocking society and the legitimate interests of young people," the chancellor emphasizes in the speech.

"The offenders will feel the full force of the law."

Tens of thousands of young people demonstrated across Germany over the weekend, mostly peacefully.

However, several of the protests were followed by sometimes severe riots, such as in Frankfurt, where stones and petrol bombs were thrown, shop windows were smashed and looting took place.

More than 100 police officers were injured.

A number of companies are expected to be affected, including carmakers Opel and Rolls-Royce, consumer goods giant Procter & Gamble, e-mobility supplier Vitesco, Daimler Truck AG and precision engineering firm Paul Beier GmbH.

Education Minister Karin Prien has said the violence that occurred in the aftermath of youth protests on Saturday evening was in part an indication that the integration of people of migrant background into German society could be improved.

Prien told broadcaster Deutschlandfunk said that the "for the most part peaceful demonstrations" had been followed by rioting by left-wing radicals "but also by others who probably come from migrant milieus."

She said that recognizing this fact was not about stirring up resentments, which she called "politically wrong," but about facing reality and getting a picture of why people resort to such means.

"And if they come from migrant milieus, we should be worried about it and look at the causes," said Prien, a member of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative Christian Democrats (CDU).

She said one question was why integration succeeds less well in some groups than in others.

"And it's not about the question of a passport. It's about the question: Why have people not been integrated into our society and what can be done so it works better in future," she said.

Her comments came despite the fact that authorities in Frankfurt, which saw the worst of the violence, said that most of the people they arrested in connection with rioting over the weekend were German citizens.

Prien's remarks came after archconservative Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU) said the "peaceful demonstrations were hijacked toward the evening by violence-prone left-wing groups and migrant anarchists," without offering evidence for who was behind the violent turn in the demonstrations.

Dobrindt's comment was, however, called into question by Defense Minister Boris Pistorius of the center-left Social Democrats (SPD), the junior partner in Germany's federal coalition government.

"What are migrant groups, then? Are these people living in Germany in the third generation who are German nationals? Where do we stop differentiating here? I think this is going in the wrong direction," he said.

Pistorius said, however, that whoever had been responsible for the rioting had to be punished for it.

His intervention comes as the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) continues, without evidence, to blame migration for most of the country's problems, with Dobrindt seeming to adopt some of the populist party's anti-migrant rhetoric.

A 34-year-old man accused of having killed two people while racing with his car through a pedestrian zone in the eastern city of Leipzig in May is going on trial on Monday.

The accused has also been charged with 85 counts of attempted murder.

State prosecutors argue that the man planned the attack with the intent of killing people with his car, which reached speeds of up to 90 kmh (56 mph) during the rampage.

The trial has been scheduled to last until July of next year.

#291. One annoying problem with the iPhone Messages app has an easy fix

Apple's iMessage can be customized to fit your needs however you like

Apple's iMessage has evolved a lot over the years. In recent updates, the Cupertino company has added everything from satellite messaging that can reach out to your emergency contact while in a remote location to aesthetic changes like customizable backgrounds. Keeping abreast of these changes can be difficult, especially when Apple releases a new iOS update every year.

Despite these updates, users often lament the inconvenience of their iMessage app arrangement. Why, for example, are applications you've never used at the top of the dropdown menu, while your most used apps remain buried at the bottom? The answer is that you likely haven't taken the time to customize the menu's layout.

Some of the most impactful changes have come through the introduction of iMessage apps. Since the introduction of iOS 18, several applications have been installed in the messaging app by default. As of the latest update, iOS 27, 14 apps are included by default. These popular applications bring features like sending your location, voice recordings, stickers, GIFs, music, photos and polls. Other applications, like ESPN and Venmo, further expand the functionalities of your messaging app. Luckily, you can keep them all ordered how you want.

Before customizing your app layout, let's quickly review how to pull up your iMessage dropdown menu. First, make sure that you have downloaded the latest iOS. Once updated, open your Messages and either tap a conversation or hit the compose button, which resembles a pencil touching a white square located at the bottom of righthand corner of your screen.

Once a conversation is pulled up, tap the Plus (+) button beside your messages. Here, you will find a full list of your available iMessage apps  . Next, hold down the app you want to move until the icon shrinks, drag it to its desired place on the dropdown menu and let go.

You can also add more apps to your iMessages. Open your phone's App Store for iMessage. Go to Messages, open a conversation, tap the Plus (+) symbol and touch the circular blue App Store icon. Once you open the App Store, you can peruse Apple's list of popular applications or search for something specific. To download a new app, simply tap the Get button next to the app's name. If the app requires purchasing it, you will see the app's price rather than a Get button. To exit the app store, swipe down or tap Close (X).

To delete individual apps you've added, or to manage the iMessage functionalities of your downloaded apps, visit your Settings app. From there, tap Apps > Messages > iMessage Apps. Here you can decide whether you want to toggle the application on or off. #290. Its harder than ever to spot fake content online. Here are some strategies.

We should all probably spend less time staring at screens. At least, that's what the professionals tell us. And yet the average person needs to be online. They use the internet for work, to pay bills, to access government resources, and to follow political leaders. Many have turned social media into their livelihoods.

And if you skip one day on the internet, you are sure to miss a year's worth of memes, references, and even historical events. In fact, social media is where more than half of Americans get their news, if not from a chatbot assistant.

It's online where you'll be lulled into doomscrolling, engage in unhealthy digital interactions, or witness violence. A good portion of what you see may not even be real. It may be trying to intentionally deceive you. For those staying online, there is at least one way to protect yourself from false information: Stop and ask why.

Why am I still scrolling? Why did this account post this particular opinion? Why is this ad targeting me? Why would this platform allow this?

Pausing is a stopgap for misinformation, media literacy experts say. A few minutes is often all it takes.

In this age of AI and misinformation, not many people are being taught the basics of consuming modern media.

"Most states don’t require districts to offer news and media literacy instruction," said Chuck Salter, president and CEO of the News Literacy Project. The News Literacy Project promotes K-12 media literacy curriculum to address growing gaps among the next generation of news consumers.

In 2023, the U.S. Surgeon General called for intentional media literacy instruction. A 2024 survey of educators by The National Association for Media Literacy Education found that only 12 percent of schools offered media literacy as part of their core curriculum. Yet news and media literacy is an essential life skill, experts argue.

How are adults faring? Around 25 percent of U.S. adults read at the lowest literacy level. When it comes to digital literacy skills, one third of U.S. workers lack basic knowledge. Around half say they find it difficult to spot fake news when scrolling online, according to a 2025 Pew Research survey.

Even the savviest social media users — who are increasingly turning to these platforms for both news and entertainment coverage — are navigating an overwhelming amount of posts aimed to deceive them.

"Social media is littered with false and misleading content," said Sofia Rubinson, Senior Editor at misinformation watchdog NewsGuard. In addition to an abundance of intentionally stimulating content, "it is inevitable to come across AI fakes, twisted political claims, and foreign disinformation when scrolling."

More than one-third of new web content is now AI-generated, according to recent data from Pew Research. Other reports allege more than half of the internet is made up of "AI slop." And estimates of the number of bot social media accounts range from 10 percent of platforms to nearly 50 percent.

Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince claims agentic bot usage constitutes 57.4 percent of total internet traffic, while human traffic has dropped to 42.6 percent.

Despite claims of free speech and open town squares by its leaders, social media isn't a neutral conveyor of information, Marijus Briedis, Chief Technology Officer of online security company NordVPN, told Mashable. "Feeds are built to move you quickly and reward things that provoke a reaction. That is a design choice, and it happens to be the exact environment where synthetic content performs best."

Many of these design choices are currently under the spotlight of federal and state regulators, including features like endless scrolls, personalized recommendation algorithms, and autoplay.

Other, less noticeable, platform choices make it worse, like the sporadic ability to embed or link to external sources on sites where users most often get their news, including TikTok and X. Without these built-in fact-checking opportunities, we're forced to rely on our own intuition.

"We scroll fast, react on instinct, and read likes and shares as 'lots of people believe this,'" explained Roei Sherman, senior director of research at cloud security firm Mitiga.  Recommended deals for you The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile Products available for purchase through affiliate links. If you buy something through links on our site, Mashable may earn an affiliate commission.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile

Our scrolling habits, combined with the algorithm's rules of engagement, are further enabled by Big Tech's ongoing moderation problem.

"You have a much more free flow of information, which has always been the case in the United States, but there's an even further lack of moderation occurring now," explained Zohaib Ahmed, CEO of deepfake detector Resemble.AI.

Large platforms like Meta and X have decimated human moderation teams in recent years, while simultaneously weathering allegations of censorship by their AI-powered moderation tools. YouTube, a hot spot for AI slop, has also loosened its moderation guidelines.

Ahmed explains that advanced AI models have pushed us further toward the "Indistinguishability Threshold," or the point at which the human senses fail to distinguish between legitimate and illegitimate content without the help of technology itself.

He adds that indistinguishability stirs confusion and conflict in online content moderation, too, especially on platforms that have slashed professional teams in favor of community fact-checking.

"That creates more commentary that can be split down the middle, that can be very opinionated and isn't very precise when it comes to labeling misinformation or disinformation," Ahmed said. "The average user will simply gloss over that, and they won't think to dig in any further than what the human moderators have already done."

The popularization of friendly chatbots and helpful AI agents have made many more susceptible to scams and manipulation, experts told Mashable.

"We tend to be far too loose with the AI agents we interact with daily," said Eyal Elazar, head of market intelligence for e-commerce security business Riskified. When it comes to scams, bad actors weaponize this psychology and count on users to let their guard down around "cutesy" personable agents, he explained.

Meanwhile, AI continues to promise the user an unburdened life. AI agents, AI-powered search engines, and chatbots encourage users to consolidate access to information into a single helpful tool. According to Elazar, the human desire for frictionless experiences, where everything is at our fingertips with a single click or one chatbot prompt, may end up being our biggest vulnerability.

"AI makes it really easy to avoid thinking for yourself," Salter said. "We have to exercise our agency."

A lot has changed in just a few years. It's easy to fake a crowd. It's cheap to run a scam. And fake media no longer looks fake, Sherman said. Now, "the instincts we built up have stopped working, and we haven't built new ones yet," Sherman said.

How do we build those new habits? We fight back by slowing down, said Andrew Jones, co-founder of AI security firm Adaptive Security.

"Social media rewards speed. Every autoplay, every infinite scroll, every push notification trains us to react in a second and move to the next post," he said. "Protecting yourself doesn’t take a technical background."

Jones said it's more important than ever to build a pause into your everyday routine, even if it take some effort. But just a few minutes sets yourself up to fight back, no matter your skills.

We need to exercise caution, experts say, but not let ourselves fall into conspiracy. Skepticism is healthy. Cynicism is dangerous, warns Salter. "It can lead us to believe what we want to or reject information that challenges us, regardless of whether it’s true," he said.

If you choose to stay online, stay tethered to the real world. Fact check information with real people you know. Discuss viral posts with your friends.

"Once people understand that anything can be faked, they start doubting the real things too," said Briedis. "You do not get that back easily."

The plan does not include a mission similar to Apollo 8 or Artemis II.

Chinese space officials confirmed this weekend that the Asian nation plans to land its astronauts on the Moon within three years.

At the Seventh Manned Spaceflight Conference in Beijing, officials, including Wang Xiang, chief designer for the lunar exploration program, laid out the country’s most publicly detailed plans yet for a series of missions leading up to a crewed lunar landing “before 2030.”

China’s lunar landings will involve a lunar-orbit rendezvous similar to what NASA did in the 1960s and early 1970s with the Apollo program. However, lacking a rocket as powerful as the Saturn V vehicle, the crew and lunar lander will launch separately to the Moon.

According to slides shared on social media, the current plan involves:

The public release of this new information provides a timeline for gauging China’s technical progress in its efforts to land humans on the Moon before 2030 and beat NASA and the United States back to the lunar surface.

Notably, the plan (for now, at least) omits a mission similar to Apollo 8 or Artemis II, which involved a crew flying out to the Moon and either entering orbit or passing close by before returning to Earth. The Mengzhou vehicle should still get a workout closer to Earth with humans on board as part of missions carrying astronauts to Tiangong, China’s space station in low-Earth orbit.

NASA has set a target of landing humans on the Moon by 2028, a year or so ahead of China. The United States, which has been working on the Space Launch System rocket for 15 years and the Orion spacecraft even longer, has a more established rocket and crew vehicle.

But there are major questions surrounding the development of a lunar lander, for which both SpaceX and Blue Origin have multibillion-dollar development contracts. Depending on how these projects go, a US lunar landing could be delayed to 2030 or even later.

For example, in August 2025, the China Manned Space Agency successfully tested a high-fidelity mock-up of its 26-ton Lanyue lunar lander. The test used giant tethers to simulate lunar gravity as the vehicle fired its main engines and fine-control thrusters to land on a cratered surface and take off from a location near Beijing.

Recently, the Mengzhou spacecraft for the 2027 test atop a Long March 10A rocket arrived at the Wenchang Space Launch Site in Hainan, China, where the mission will launch.

US government assessments of the Chinese space program are restricted, but lawmakers are clearly taking the threat seriously. In the last 12 months, the US Congress and White House have given broad latitude to NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman to streamline the Artemis Program to land humans on the Moon. He has moved swiftly to cancel the Lunar Gateway space station and planned upgrades to the Space Launch System rocket. And just last week, Isaacman announced plans to help Blue Origin develop a lunar lander by finding a way to boost the Orion spacecraft into low-lunar orbit.

“We have the mandate, we have the resources, and the support from our stakeholders to be able to execute, and that’s what we intend to do,” he said at the time.

For a couple of years, it has been clear that China has made a major commitment to landing astronauts on the Moon, preferably before the United States returns to the lunar surface, to score a major geopolitical win. Beyond this near-term competition, both NASA and China’s space program are building capabilities to establish a long-term presence at the Moon’s South Pole. As part of this second phase of the contest, Isaacman committed NASA to the development of a base on the surface of the Moon over the next decade.

#286. Gemini could be poking through your emails - here's how to stop it

To think "Don't be evil" used to be Google's motto.

So, is Google feeding your emails to Gemini? The answer is both yes and no. To execute these tasks, Gemini inherently needs access to the content of your emails. The real issue is whether your data migrates beyond these select uses.

Google released a statement in April 2026 detailing Gemini's interaction with your data. It says that "Google does not train its foundational AI models, including Gemini, on your personal emails." Instead, Gemini only accesses your inbox for "isolated tasks," such as summarizing emails or drafting responses. As Google explains, this means that Gemini "only processes your information to complete your specific request, and doesn't hold onto that data afterward." In other words, Gemini's analysis of your emails is localized within your personal use of the applications.

Google's support page clarifies that such safeguards extend beyond your emails and include Workspace apps like Chat, Calendar, Docs, Drive, Sheets and Slides. It states: "We do not use your Workspace data to train or improve the underlying generative AI and large language models that power Gemini, Search, and other systems outside of Workspace without permission."

"Without permission" is a key caveat here — the permissions change once you link Google's content apps across your account. For instance, Google notes that, when you connect content apps from Google Workspace to Search services, which can enable AI Mode features, it may "use that data to improve Google services for everyone, including by training generative AI models."

However, Google also says Search services "do not train generative AI models directly on your Gmail inbox." Rather, "when you interact with Search, summaries, excerpts, generated media, and inferences from your relevant media, emails, and files may be used to help us answer your prompts. To make our responses relevant, helpful, and high quality, we train our generative AI models off of these summaries, excerpts, generated media, and inferences."

To turn off Gemini, go to your Gmail account and visit Settings. If you're using the app, tap the three lines at the top left corner, scroll down, select Settings and choose your email. Go to Smart features and deselect the box. To remove Gemini from your Workspace apps, tap Google Workspace smart features and clear the checkboxes. These settings apply across your account, so you only need to go through this process once.

In a web browser, click on the Settings button (gear icon) beside your search bar at the top right side. This will bring up a dropdown menu displaying various quick settings. At the top of this dropdown, select See all settings. From here, scroll through your General tab until you find Smart features. Uncheck the box and confirm your choice. Then go back to the General tab, navigate to Google Workspace smart features, click Manage Workspace smart feature settings, turn off both options and click Save.

Unfortunately, there are downsides to disabling Gemini: turning off smart features can also switch off things like spelling and grammar checks. Perhaps as a means of incentivizing users to adopt its AI, Google puts its customers in the uncomfortable position of choosing between basic editing software and potentially invasive features. As a result, you may need to either suffer through meddlesome AI functionalities or learn to trust your own grammatical acuity.

If you don't want to lose these AI features but want to limit what Google uses to train its AI, you can change your Search Services History and Personalized Recommendations settings. By default, your Search Services History and Personalized Recommendations settings are set to your most recent Web & App Activity and Search Personalization settings.

To turn off your Search Services History, sign in to your Google account and go to your Search Services History settings. Here, you choose whether you'd like to turn it off. You can also delete your previously saved activity. To leave the setting on and restrict what it saves, you can adjust your Save Media settings.

#285. This Samsung Galaxy problem sadly still exists in 2026, but you can easily fix it

Samsung still loads Galaxy phones with apps you might never use.

I recently upgraded from a Google Pixel to a Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra, and the difference in preloaded apps was noticeable. My Pixel cam with plenty of Google's software, most of which I used anyways, but the Galaxy has a longer list of apps I had no interest in opening. It seems that $1,400 isn't enough to get an uncluttered app drawer.

Those unwanted extras are bloatware: preinstalled software that you don't really want. Such apps clutter your phone, consume storage space and sometimes bother you with notifications too. The specific list of apps will differ depending on the Galaxy model, region and carrier, so your app drawer out of the box may look significantly different from someone else's. Fortunately, many of these unwanted apps can be removed or disabled in a few taps.

This isn't a new complaint. The Galaxy S4 was criticized for having a small amount of usable storage back in 2013, for example. Its 16GB version reportedly left buyers with about 9.5GB usable, mostly because of Android, Samsung's system software and bundled apps. Samsung has since allowed its users to remove or disable many preinstalled apps, but the clutter remains.

You may come across Samsung Shop, Samsung TV Plus and Samsung Global Goals, which are optional apps offered by Samsung. Depending on where you buy your Galaxy, third-party additions can include Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, OneDrive and Spotify. There are some that might even be worth keeping: if you already use Microsoft's cloud storage, you'd want OneDrive installed anyway. But if you keep everything you need in Google Drive, another cloud app isn't adding much.

Swipe up from the home screen to show your app list, press and hold an app that you don't use and then select Uninstall if it's available. You can also go to Settings > Apps, select the app and uninstall it from there. This removes the app and frees up the storage it occupies.

Some preinstalled apps won't allow that. Instead, go to the app's page in Settings > Apps and find Disable. This will prevent the app from running and hide its icon, but its files will still be on your phone. You can undo the process by going back to the same menu and tapping Enable.

If you're still stuck with an unwanted app, touch and hold an empty area of the Home screen, tap Settings and select Hide apps (or Hide apps on Home and Apps screens). Select the apps you want to hide and then hit Done. This will make their icons disappear from view, but the apps remain installed and can still send notifications.

To turn off those notifications for hidden apps, go to Settings > Notifications > App notifications, choose the hidden app and disable Allow notifications. At least you won't hear from something you never even wanted.

Keep in mind that hiding an app and turning off its notifications won't free up storage or revoke its permissions. Samsung's official instructions for disabling preinstalled apps also note that menu options may vary based on the device and software version. Avoid disabling unfamiliar system services. You can't delete core apps like Phone, Messages, Contacts, Gallery and My Files.

#283. Claude’s new rules against game cloning won’t stop the AI copying boom

The tsunami of imitators is way bigger than any one model maker can stem.

Last week, Anthropic introduced a new system prompt designed to stop its Claude models from re-creating specific, existing video games. While that move could help shield Anthropic from some liability, it’s unlikely to slow much of the massive wave of AI-assisted game porting and copying that has emerged in recent months.

A social media user and AI decompilation enthusiast going by the name “chasm” was among the first to note the prompt change late last week, saying a new rule seemed to be added to the Claude Code prompt on or around October 27. That rule—included in a json file under the name “tengu_heron_brook”—reads as follows:

Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user’s own designs and assets. Don’t build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original.

XDA later independently verified that the new rule appears in version 2.1.314 of the Claude Code binary, which was released on October 30. XDA also reported that the “tengu_heron_brook” rule had been used for other purposes in earlier versions and that the Claude Opus 5.5 model specifically seemed to have its own distinct and independent instructions restricting game recreations as part of its system prompt bundle.

Following chasm’s initial report, Anthropic software engineer Addy Osmani confirmed on social media that the company had “added two sentences to Claude Code’s prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else’s specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy.”

He added that the new prompt was designed to still allow “original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets,” even as a handful of issue reports on Anthropic’s GitHub suggest the new prompt is getting in the way of some game development use cases.

We added two sentences to Claude Code’s prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else’s specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy.

Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to keep working.

We’ll continue to iterate to ensure we’re striking the right balance. In the meantime, if Claude turns down something that’s yours, send it my way.

— Addy Osmani (@addyosmani) October 30, 2026

Anthropic’s new prompt comes as AI coding tools are powering a deluge of game projects based on existing work in one way or another. That includes thrown-together copies of game demos that are making some developers afraid to show their early work publicly, as well as thousands of AI-powered decompilation and porting projects for retro games. Thanks to AI tools, what used to be a time-consuming process requiring painstaking human effort is now orders of magnitude more efficient (though some veteran coders complain that these vibe-coded ports and decomp projects fail to clear the same quality bar as human-centered efforts).

The trend has gotten so bad that decomp.dev—a years-old community devoted to the “brutally difficult, time-consuming task” of game decompilation—announced it was shutting down last month. Community maintainer Luke Street wrote that quickly improving AI tools had made it clear that “community aspect of decompilation has been broken” as newcomers “rac[e] to port games, especially utilizing decompilations that they did not contribute to.”

“Decomp.dev was originally designed to gamify decompilation: watching the progress go up was a fun way to stay motivated when every fraction of a percent took real human effort,” Street wrote. “Today, that same idea has warped decompilation into a hollow numbers game, exacerbated by folks who just want to burn tokens to make number go up or ‘port game to PC,’ all else be damned.

While Anthropic’s new prompt can be seen as a noble effort to push back against the flood of AI-powered, vibe-coded copying, it seems unlikely to have much impact overall. That’s primarily because eager game copiers can simply shift to any of the other frontier models that haven’t introduced such restrictions. And even if the AI industry as a whole began to bar this kind of use case, coders could switch to cheaper open-weight models that aren’t subject to these kinds of restrictions and are not all that far behind in capabilities.

The prompt may have a more immediate benefit for Anthropic, helping protect the company from potential liability for copyright infringement in these projects. We’ve seen how AI companies face legal headaches if their models generate images based on copyrighted works, for instance. As Osmani noted in confirming the new anti-game copying prompt, “Using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy”—a policy that’s surely in place to protect the company legally.

Decompilation efforts based on reverse engineering code generally pass legal muster as long as “expressive elements” like art and sound assets are not included in the project. But there’s no guarantee that individual vibe-coders using Claude would be so careful with their efforts, even with Anthropic guardrails against IP theft in place.

On the other hand, there’s a risk that Anthropic’s efforts could prove too restrictive, limiting transformative game projects that build off existing work. Take, for instance, the increasingly popular trend of using AI to merge two different game concepts into one, adding Mario to Elden Ring or Spider-Man to Batman: Arkham Knight, for instance. Are these the kinds of “recreations of a specific existing game” that Claude’s new prompt should block? Or are they transformative works that are legally and creatively distinct from what inspired them? And how does the use of copyright-protected characters and images factor in?

Beyond mashups, how should a model like Claude ensure there’s a difference between a direct re-creation of Tetris (ostensibly disallowed by the new prompt) and a mere game in the Tetris genre (ostensibly allowed by the prompt)?

These are issues that even courts can have trouble adjudicating in the best circumstances. Asking an AI model to reliably draw the line between acceptable and unacceptable game clones is a tall order, even with a new two-sentence prompt in place.

#282. Think twice before putting your gaming console inside a cabinet

Cabinets are a great way to keep your game console hot, which is terrible for it.

One of the reasons often cited for the failure of the original Xbox in Japan is that the console (and its original bulky controller) was too big for many Japanese homes. Now, there was more to it, such as a lack of the genres and franchises Japanese gamers preferred. But this highlights an important point that space matters; some modern consoles could be an awkward fit if you're living in a cramped studio apartment.

Even in the West, gamers often need to optimize the space around their TV to make it livable for everyone in the home. Aside from comfort, you might be worried about style, aiming for a sleek, minimalist look. And while it may seem like a great idea on the surface, you certainly shouldn't jam any of the latest consoles into a cabinet in your entertainment center.

That might seem counterintuitive, since AV gear is often what those cabinets are for. But doing so could hamper your console's performance or shorten its lifespan. That's a potentially expensive mistake with memory prices inflating console costs by hundreds of dollars.

The primary concern here is heat. A modern console like the PlayStation 5 is a far more power-hungry device than your Blu-ray player or cable box. It's rendering real-time 3D graphics and physics, and the hardware necessary to power that consumes a lot of energy. During a game, the standard PS5 can consume up to 220W, a figure roughly matched by the Xbox Series X. Conversely, even Panasonic's relatively high-end UB820 Blu-ray player isn't going to hit any more than 32W.

Consoles have fans to expel heat and vents to take in cold air, but this can't flow well when the system is in a cabinet. The hot air can end up trapped, while it might not have enough room to draw in new air, so it cycles the same hot air. When your console is surrounded by heat like this, it forces the fans to work harder to maintain a safe internal temperature. Your system also might scale back performance to reduce heat production. Under extreme conditions, prolonged heat can trigger visual glitches or force the console to temporarily shut down to avoid damaging its components.

Closely related to this is the issue of dust. Although a cabinet can block some material from getting in, it also make it harder for particles to escape. As with any device, a thick enough layer will trap heat by reducing airflow out of vents or how much air can be taken in. This leads to the same problems and can reduce the lifespan of your console.

For proper ventilation, Sony recommends leaving about 4 inches (about 10 centimeters) of clearance around a PlayStation. Microsoft is a little more aggressive with the Xbox, proposing 4 to 6 inches (up to 15 centimeters) on all sides. Nintendo simply advises docking the Switch 2 in an "open, ventilated area."

The same principles apply to PC-based systems too, such as the ASUS ROG Ally X or Valve Steam Machine. While every system takes in and expels air at different places, a trapped space is never good. You should also avoid putting controllers, game cases, books or similar items on top of a console, as that will block its vents. Don't keep your console near a heat source, either.

If space is at a premium, some airflow is better than nothing. Remember that the PS5 and Xbox Series consoles can both be placed vertically or horizontally, so experiment with what fits into your setup. You might even consider aiming a small fan toward the console to help air circulate. It's also a good idea to periodically dust the outside of your console using a microfiber cloth and can of compressed air. If you use canned air, be sure to hold it level and several inches away from your hardware. Otherwise, you might spray liquids onto circuitry.

None of this is too complicated. Rather, console makers don't put it front-and-center in their instructions, which they probably should. Gaming hardware has come a long way since people were jamming the 9W NES on a shelf to play Super Mario Bros and Zelda.

#280. Why some websites are blocking AI agents from accessing the web

Amazon is blocking rival shopping agents, and even websites that welcome AI assistants can stop them with an ordinary CAPTCHA.

An AI agent can take over your grocery shopping, right up until a website asks it to prove it's human. That's the problem Meta's Muse has encountered at Walmart (one of its retail partners), which says the verification checks weren't intended to stop the assistant. Amazon has been more direct, deliberately blocking the tool from shopping on its site, according to TechCrunch.

The appeal of personal AI agents like Meta's Muse is that these assistants can navigate websites, fill shopping carts and book travel instead of handing you recommendations and leaving the rest to you. However, giving an agent permission to act on your behalf doesn't mean a website has agreed to deal with it. Some restrictions are deliberate, while others come from security systems that can't reliably distinguish legitimate agents from unwanted automated traffic. Either way, you could end up back at the keyboard doing the very task you wanted to avoid.

Security is a bigger concern when money is involved. During JPMorgan Chase's October earnings call, CFO Jeremy Barnum said some agents use shared login credentials and screen scraping to transfer funds, methods he described as "not secure." The bank blocks those methods where possible, and Barnum warned that customers who hand over their credentials could be responsible if an agent takes an unwanted action. A botched grocery order is annoying enough, but an unauthorized bank transfer is a different kind of headache.

Amazon is also battling Perplexity over its Comet AI browser. The retailer argues that the agent violates its access rules and puts customer data at risk, while Perplexity maintains that users have authorized it to act. A federal appeals court vacated a preliminary injunction against Perplexity in August 2026, although the underlying dispute remains unresolved. There's also an interesting wrinkle: Amazon has its own Buy for Me feature that can purchase products from other brands' websites.

Businesses have commercial reasons to control automated access, too. eBay's user agreement prohibits unauthorized buy-for-me agents unless the company grants permission. Delta told TechCrunch it has no integration allowing third-party agents to book flights through its website, although the airline did not confirm whether it deliberately blocks specific agents.

Walmart's experience shows why a blocked agent isn't necessarily the result of a deliberate ban. Human-verification prompts can interrupt automated shopping sessions, while Zillow has acknowledged that its anti-scraping defenses sometimes catch agents it otherwise permits. From the user's perspective, both can look like an assistant that simply can't finish the job.

Anyone who's browsed through a VPN might recognize the routine. Google explains that shared VPN networks can trigger reCAPTCHA challenges when their traffic resembles automated activity. AI agents can encounter similar checks simply by navigating a website, even when following someone's instructions. Switching on a VPN won't magically override a site's restrictions on automated access, either.

Cloudflare, which previously introduced controls against AI web crawlers, now lets website owners distinguish between search crawlers, AI training bots and agents acting on behalf of users. Since September 15, new domains using Cloudflare have defaulted to allowing search crawlers while blocking AI training bots and agents on pages displaying ads. Website owners can adjust those rules, meaning a site blocking AI training bots isn't necessarily rejecting an assistant trying to buy something. Other platforms are taking a more controlled approach. Shopify's checkout tools let compatible browser agents update checkout details and submit orders after buyer confirmation, with control handed back to shoppers for required authentication steps.
