#278. For US Democrats, climate policy is now about energy bills

Climate change has all but disappeared from Democrats' campaign pitches, replaced by promises to lower electricity bills. So what would the party really do for climate policy should it win control of Congress?

President Donald Trump's administration has gutted US climate policy. Yet, even as wildfires, record heat waves and flooding hit communities across the country, Democrats are keeping quiet about global warming on the midterm campaign trail.

Instead, candidates are packaging climate policy as an affordability issue, stressing how Americans are struggling to afford gas, groceries and to insure their homes against climate-fueled weather extremes.

Take James Talarico, who represents the Democratic Party's best chance at winning a senate race in the Republican stronghold of Texas in nearly 40 years. Though he makes some mention of climate change on his campaign's "energy and environment" page, that is not his focus.

His pledges center on lowering energy costs, providing emergency relief for spiking utility bills, making data centers pay for their own grid upgrades and growing energy sector jobs.

This aligns with analysis from nonprofit news organization Inside Climate News showing that the Democrats have dramatically reduced mentions of climate change in their press releases and campaign messaging.

"We've entered an interesting space where climate policy doesn't need to be called climate policy to be climate policy," Max Frankel, executive director of the SEEC Institute, a nonprofit that helps guide climate policy in Congress, told DW.

Most forecasts project Democrats winning the House and a narrow majority in the Senate in the November 3 election. But without control of the White House, passing any legislation will be difficult and almost any climate policy will have to be a bipartisan endeavor, say analysts.

Given that and the Democrats' messaging-shift to affordability over climate, few experts expect a fully resurrected Inflation Reduction Act. Introduced under the Democrats to create incentives for building clean energy projects, the legislation was largely decimated by President Trump's major tax law.

But Democrats may try to bring back some climate-friendly IRA provisions, particularly measures aimed at lowering household energy costs, analysts told DW. Those include incentives for home energy-efficiency upgrades and appliances like heat pumps to replace oil and gas heaters that typically help bring down household energy bills.

Politicians could also expand an IRA manufacturing tax credit for solar, batteries, and critical minerals that largely survived. One bipartisan bill proposes extending it to include nuclear fusion components.

"It's not going to be anything at the scale of the IRA," Adrian Deveny, founder of Climate Vision, a policy firm dedicated to decarbonization, told DW. "It's like singles and doubles as opposed to a home run, which is still worth doing."

In a rare area of agreement between the parties, some Democrats and Republicans are already backing a reform bill they're hoping to pass before a new Congress is sworn in January.

If enacted, the bill could make it significantly easier to build major infrastructure projects in the US, including long-distance transmission lines that carry electricity between regions but that currently take years to build because of complex permitting rules.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"The biggest beneficiary of building more transmission will be wind and solar power, because the best and cheapest way to generate wind and solar energy tends to be far away from cities," said David Spence, a political scientist at the University of Texas who researches the politics of energy regulation. "And so, they need transmission to get their product to market."

But environmental groups say the bill could also speed up the approval of fossil fuel projects.

If Democrats win big in the midterms there might be some "peeling off their support for that bill because they think they can do better in the next Congress," said Spence.

Major new federal climate legislation is a long shot before the 2028 presidential election. And afterwards it would likely require Democrats winning the White House, the Senate and the House. While no 2028 platforms have been released yet, policy experts expect a few ideas to feature prominently.

One is data centers. Opposition to the energy-guzzling infrastructure being built en masse to power the AI boom is mounting across the country. Half of Americans are now against data centers being built close to their homes, according to a pollfrom news outlet Politico.

"I'm sure every candidate is going to have a platform with a focus on data center constraints on some level, as a way to address affordability," Deveny, who led negotiations on the IRA, said. "And that's the entry point for climate policy."

There are several ideas currently circulating — including a proposal by Democrats Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to pause data center construction — as well as ending tax breaks for data centers and imposing new taxes on their electricity use.

Democrats may also seek to restore the IRA's clean energy tax incentives. This year, more than 150 legislators co-sponsored the so-called Energy Bills Relief Act designed to reinstate IRA clean energy tax incentives, reform how transmission permits are granted, and make data centers pay for the grid upgrades they need. The bill is unlikely to pass anytime soon but offers a window into what Democrats might support.

"By far, the biggest consensus — to the extent there's anything remotely resembling a consensus — is restoring a lot of the clean energy tax incentives from the IRA," Deveny said. "Not everybody supports that but it is a highly supported idea amongst most congressional Democrats."

Support for other proposals include a new federal program to help insurers cover climate-driven disasters and bring down hefty premiums, as well as so-called climate superfunds. This would require fossil fuel companies to contribute to the costs of damage caused by extreme weather and adapting to the risks of climate change.

Vermont and New York both passed legislation to create funds, although a federal judge blocked New York's.

The 2028 presidential race is expected to begin a few weeks after the midterms end, bringing a fresh round of policy ideas and debates. A new president typically gets to drive the legislative agenda in the beginning of their term if their party also wins Congress.

"As long as the consensus is that clean energy is the cheaper source of energy, and it's going to provide stability over the long term for high energy costs — there's a million ways you can propose solutions through that lens," Deveny said.

People who worked on Apple’s robotic projects told The Information that the AI-driven home robot, code-named J595, could be named HomeView Ultra in line with Apple’s new HomeView stationary smart display. The earliest prototypes of the home robot first came out in 2018 and received approval from former Apple CEO Tim Cook to continue the project. From a technical and safety standpoint, Apple’s initial focus on a limited-purpose home robot still makes much more sense right now than any attempt to develop a general-purpose autonomous robot that could pose greater risks when operating near humans. #276. What OPEC's surprise oil cut means for gas prices

OPEC and its allies’ surprise move to slash oil production will soon be felt at US gas pumps.

The group known as OPEC+ announced Sunday it would cut oil production by more than 1.6 million barrels a day starting in May, running through the end of the year. The news sent both Brent crude futures, the global oil benchmark, and WTI, the US benchmark, up about 6% in trading Monday.

The production cut announcement also had an immediate impact on gasoline futures, which will be passed onto US drivers much more quickly than the spike in oil prices. RBOB, the most closely watched wholesale gasoline price, was up about 8 cents a gallon, or about 3%, in morning trading.

“I think OPEC is reawakening the inflation monster,” said Tom Kloza, global head of energy analysis for OPIS, which tracks gas prices for AAA. “The White House has to be shocked and major-time pissed. It certainly alters the calculus for a while.”

The national average for US gas prices stood at $3.51, on Monday, according to AAA. Kloza said he could see it getting up to $3.80 to $3.90 in relatively short order thanks to the move by OPEC.

“We’re not going to get back to $5 a gallon. I don’t think we’re even going as high as $4,” he said. But he said by the end of the summer US drivers could be back above year-earlier prices, especially if there is a hurricane or other storms affecting production along the Gulf Coast.

The average US regular gas price a year ago stood at $4.19 a gallon in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the disruption that caused to world’s energy markets. Prices eventually reached a record $5.02 a gallon on June 14, before starting a slow but steady decline over the course of more than three months during which the average price fell every day. The decline was partly driven by the release of oil from the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve, and partly by concerns that there could be a US or global recession that reduced the demand for gasoline.

Oil prices surge after OPEC+ producers announce surprise cuts

Even at $3.51, US gas prices were just below the $3.53 average on Feb. 23, 2022, the day before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

Kloza said one thing keeping prices from getting anywhere near the record levels of 2022 is that the US plans additional releases from the SPR, and US oil production and refining capacity are both up. But a cut of 1 million barrels a day of oil by OPEC+ will not be easy to make up.

“They have ability to cut production and they seem motivated to do so,” he said.

#274. Your Apple AirPods' chirping noise doesn't just mean low battery

It could indicate other things, but you can turn it off if you want to.

Have you ever heard your AirPods chirp randomly even though you weren't doing anything? The most common reason why your AirPods are trying to get your attention is that they're low in battery. You can easily check if that's what's going on by flipping their case open and looking at the phone they're paired with. However, your AirPods could be emitting sounds due to other reasons, and those sounds could range from cute little chirps to ear-piercing screeches.

Sometimes, your AirPods will keep on chirping even after being plugged in due to power fluctuations, interruptions to the electricity flowing into the device and other battery issues. Another possible reason for your AirPods chirping is connectivity issues with their paired device. If you've switched off Bluetooth on your iPhone, for instance, you'll most likely hear your AirPods make some noise. If you have your AirPods out and accidentally rub them together, you may hear them make a sound, as well.

Or, it could be for no reason at all. Apple's AirPods Pro 2 and AirPods Pro 3 support a clinical-grade Hearing Aid feature. The company says on its website that they may "periodically play a quiet chime when they're in their charging case" in order to ensure that their microphones and speakers are "operating at their best" and can provide high-quality hearing test results.

Sometimes, the sounds they emit could be harsher and more intense. They make louder, more persistent sounds if their Find My feature is triggered. That way, it'll be easier to find them, in case you've misplaced them. However, they could also produce piercing feedback noises if they've had water damage or if they get clogged with gunk and dirt. If the earbud tips of your AirPods Pro don't fit your ears well, they could also emit high-pitched noises. The AirPods Pro ship with multiple in-ear silicone tips, and you could probably get a perfect fit with one of the sizes. But if none of them fit you well enough so that the AirPods can create a seal when you wear them, you may have to buy third-party ear tips. You could also take your device to the Apple Store to get looked at.

You might not be able to stop them from making high-pitched noises in certain cases, like when there's water damage, but you can prevent your AirPods from making chirping sounds. To do so, open the AirPods case and then go to Settings on their connected device, like your iPhone. From there, tap on the device's name — typically [your name]'s AirPods — and then go to the Audio & Routing section. You'll find an option there that says Enable Charging Case Sounds. Simply toggle that setting off, and you're done.

#272. Scientists film deepest ever fish on seabed off Japan

Sign up for CNN’s Wonder Theory science newsletter. Explore the universe with news on fascinating discoveries, scientific advancements and more.

Cruising at a depth of 8,336 meters (over 27,000 feet) just above the seabed, a young snailfish has become the deepest fish ever filmed by scientists during a probe into the abyss of the northern Pacific Ocean.

Scientists from University of Western Australia and Tokyo University of Marine Science and Technology released footage of the snailfish on Sunday filmed last September by sea robots in deep trenches off Japan.

Along with the filming the deepest snailfish, the scientists physically caught two other specimens at 8,022 meters and set another record for the deepest catch.

Previously, the deepest snailfish ever spotted was at 7,703 meters in 2008, while scientists had never been able to collect fish from anywhere below 8,000 meters.

“What is significant is that it shows how far a particular type of fish will descend in the ocean,” said marine biologist Alan Jamieson, founder of the Minderoo-UWA Deep Sea Research Centre, who led the expedition.

Scientists are filming in the trenches off Japan as part of a 10-year study into the deepest fish populations in the world. Snailfish are members of Liparidae family, and while most snailfish live in shallow water, others survive at some of the greatest depths ever recorded, Jamieson said.

During the two-month survey last year, three “landers” – automatic sea robots fitted with high-resolution cameras – were dropped into three trenches – the Japan, Izu-Ogasawara and Ryukyu trenches – at varying depths.

In the Izu-Ogasawara trench, footage showed the deepest snailfish hovering calmly alongside other crustaceans on the seabed.

Jamieson classified the fish as a juvenile and said younger deep sea snailfish often stay as deep as possible to avoid being eaten by bigger predators that swim at shallower depths.

Another clip shot at between 7,500 and 8,200 meters in the same trench showed a colony of fish and crustaceans munching at bait tied to an undersea robot.

Images of the two captured snailfish – identified as Pseudoliparis belyaevi – provide a rare glimpse of the unique features that help the deep sea species survive the extreme environment.

They have tiny eyes, a translucent body, and their lack of swim bladder, which helps other fish float, works to their advantage, Jamieson said.

The professor said the Pacific Ocean is particularly conducive to vibrant activity due to its warm southern current, which encourages sea creatures to go deeper, while its abundant marine life provides a good source of food for bottom feeders.

Scientists would like to know more about creatures living at extreme depths, but cost is the constraint, Jamieson said, adding that each lander alone costs them $200,000 to assemble and operate.

“The challenges are that technology has been expensive and scientists don’t have a lot of money,” he said.

#271. Will renewed conflict derail Ethiopia's economic growth?

Ethiopia's economy is growing strongly. But renewed fighting in the north of the BRICS member state could deter investment, strain public finances and push up the cost of living.

Ethiopia's economy is growing strongly. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) forecasts real growth of 9.2% for the 2025–26 fiscal year. But renewed fighting in the north, high reconstruction costs and climate-related crop problems are threatening the country's economic recovery.

London-based financial analyst Abdulmenan Mohammed warns of the consequences of further escalation. "If there is a major conflict [...] the current economic growth will not be sustainable," he told DW.

The war that raged in Tigray and other parts of Ethiopia between 2020 and 2022 inflicted extensive damage. Infrastructure was destroyed, businesses lost production capacity and agricultural land could no longer be cultivated in some areas.

A World Bank-backed damage and needs assessment puts the damage caused by several conflicts in Ethiopia between November 2020 and December 2021 at more than $22.6 billion (€20.2 billion). Economic losses amounted to around $6 billion. The estimated bill for reconstruction and economic recovery stands at approximately $19.7 billion, which covers the total funding needed, not annual costs or damage caused by the current escalation.

A reconstruction plan covered the period from 2023 to 2028. However, it remains uncertain whether the work can be fully funded and completed within that timeframe.

Financial analyst Abdulmenan Mohammed believes the economic consequences of the Tigray war were even more severe. In addition to the direct destruction, he points to lost economic output, high inflation and foreign currency shortages at the time. International trade conditions also deteriorated: in 2022, Ethiopia lost its benefits under the US African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA), which had allowed certain African exports to enter the US market duty-free.

Following the Pretoria peace agreement in November 2022, the economy began to recover. According to the IMF, it grew by 7.2% in 2022–23 and 8.1% in 2023–24. The organization puts growth at 9.2% for 2024–25 and forecasts a further 9.2% for 2025–26. Agriculture, mining and electricity generation are among the main drivers.

This does not contradict the economic damage caused by the war. Gross domestic product (GDP) measures the total economic output of a country. If major sectors outside conflict-affected areas continue to expand, the overall economy can grow even while individual regions are still suffering the consequences of violence.

However, high growth rates do not mean that the country's economic problems have been resolved. Reconstruction remains a major challenge, inflation continues to put pressure on households and the government has to service its debt. In late 2023, Ethiopia defaulted after missing an interest payment on a Eurobond. Reforms supported by an IMF program launched in 2024 are intended to address structural weaknesses in the economy.

A renewed escalation could put additional pressure on public finances. The government would have to spend more on military personnel, equipment and logistics. At the same time, economic activity and, consequently, tax revenues could decline in the affected regions.

"A substantial share of government resources would be tied up in military spending that would otherwise be available for infrastructure, education and social services," warned Abdulmenan Mohammed. The extent of this impact would depend on the scale and duration of any renewed conflict.

A prolonged war could also prompt businesses to postpone investments. International lenders and donors might become more cautious, while the government would need additional funds for security and humanitarian assistance. This could leave less money available for roads, energy infrastructure and other development projects.

The IMF forecasts an average inflation rate of 11.7% for 2025–26. Prices are therefore expected to continue rising, although at a slower pace than in previous years.

Abdulmenan Mohammed expects a further escalation to intensify inflationary pressures. "If the conflict escalates further, inflation is likely to rise," he said. To finance additional spending, the government might resort to more domestic borrowing. This could crowd out private businesses by making it harder for them to access credit and finance investments.

The military also needs foreign currency to purchase equipment from abroad. If this demand increases, fewer foreign exchange reserves could be available to private businesses for imports. This would put further pressure on the birr exchange rate and drive up the cost of imported goods, fuel and industrial inputs.

The extent of these effects on the BRICS member state would also depend on export earnings, monetary policy and developments in international markets. A new surge in inflation is therefore a risk, but not an inevitable consequence of the escalation. A combination of rising prices and uncertain incomes would be particularly difficult for poorer households.

Abdulmenan Mohammed sees agriculture, as well as the tourism and hospitality sectors, as particularly vulnerable. "Agriculture is especially exposed because much of the fighting takes place in rural areas where farmers work," he said.

Insecurity around farmland, disrupted transport routes and shortages of agricultural inputs can undermine production. At the same time, parts of the country are experiencing insufficient rainfall and poor harvest prospects. Failed harvests reduce farmers' incomes, while lower food supplies can push prices even higher.

Tourism is also highly sensitive to security risks. Travel advisories and reports of fighting can deter visitors, reducing revenues for hotels and tour operators.

When making investment decisions, international investors consider not only market size but also political stability, security and the reliability of state institutions. A further escalation could therefore delay investment decisions or prompt companies to consider alternative locations.

However, there is currently no concrete evidence that companies are already withdrawing investments from Ethiopia because of the fighting and relocating them to neighboring countries such as Kenya. Abdulmenan Mohammed also sees no demonstrable economic advantage for Kenya at this stage. Beyond security, factors such as tax administration, public services and governance also play a decisive role.

#269. Most of our measures of a key cognitive process don't agree

A big study with very little beyond negative results still gets published.

It’s widely acknowledged that it’s nearly impossible to publish negative results in scientific journals. “We didn’t see anything” is a much harder sell than finding that a hypothesis is clearly right. Findings of no effect tend to either be shuffled off to low-profile journals or left behind as unpublished lab lore.

The high-profile journal Nature, however, made a notable exception this week, publishing a study that tells us that a bunch of methods we have been using to try to measure a key emotional ability don’t seem to be measuring the same thing. The results mean that we don’t have a good way to measure the impact of a concept that is the basis of a key method in therapy.

One of the most successful forms of therapy is cognitive behavioral therapy, or CBT. In part, CBT is based on getting people to step back and engage in “cognitive reappraisal.” This requires people to think over a situation that has caused a negative emotional response and find ways to reinterpret it so that it has less impact on them. The ability to engage in this process has been linked to emotional resilience.

Given its importance, a lot of studies have looked at what’s going on in the brain when people engage in cognitive reappraisal. There are also a number of questionnaires that are thought to measure a person’s capacity to engage in the process. So, a large international collaboration of researchers decided to look at these more carefully. “We focused on three widely used indices that are often assumed to reflect related facets of reappraisal capacity: trait questionnaires, task-based affective ratings following reappraisal, and amygdala down-regulation during reappraisal,” they wrote.

The amygdala is a structure deep in the brain that tends to be active when people have emotional responses to events (as well as in a wide variety of additional circumstances). So, it makes sense to expect that it would be less active if people were trying to tone down their emotions. But to find out whether that’s actually correct, you need to look at brain activity. Here, the team relied on 40 functional MRI data sets, providing a large enough data set to tease out even relatively small effects.

Which is a good thing, because the effects really were hard to detect. “The effect size was comparatively small: To detect this effect size with a statistical power of 80 percent, a single study would need to test 1,105 participants,” the researchers note, going on to say that very few fMRI studies have access to anywhere near that many subjects.

But there were even bigger problems when the differences among individuals in the MRI data were compared to their differences in the questionnaires or task-based ratings. Almost none of the variance in the different measures correlated with each other. We could go through the numbers, but a figure from the paper makes the issue quite clear.

Further issues became apparent when the researchers started looking at activity in the areas of the brain that are responsible for high-level decision-making. If people were really engaging their ability to re-evaluate emotional triggers, presumably these areas should be active, as they are needed to power the re-evaluation process.

But that wasn’t what the fMRI data showed. Instead, there was a correlation between the response of the amygdala and the response elsewhere in the brain. In other words, if the amygdala was very active, implying a stronger emotional response, then activity in the decision-making areas of the brain was also higher. If the emotional response seemed tamped down, then activity in the reasoning centers was lower as well.

In a bit of an understatement, the researchers declared, “These findings call for a fundamental reassessment of how reappraisal capacity is measured and interpreted across behavioural and neural levels of analysis.”

The primary issue is that these three ways of looking at emotional regulation were thought to be exploring the same thing, but it’s clear that they’re not. As the researchers point out, this probably shouldn’t be viewed as a surprise. The questionnaires typically ask about overall personality tendencies, and so cover a very long time period. The answers are also likely to implicate a variety of traits beyond simple emotional control.

Both the task-based ratings and fMRI work, by contrast, capture in-the-moment responses. But they do so under very, very different experimental circumstances—namely, one of them involves being stuffed in an MRI tube. Beyond that, many of the fMRI experiments involve simplifying the process of emotional regulation in order to get consistent data. It’s entirely possible that these differences also influence brain activity in a variety of ways.

So, the take-home appears to be that re-evaluation of emotional responses may be a real phenomenon, but we don’t currently have tools that can clearly capture the process effectively. Gaining that ability may require developing new methods, and thinking more clearly about what different stages of the re-evaluation process require. In the meantime, the people behind this work caution that “strong claims about a person’s emotion regulation capacity based on any specific brain region should be made with considerable caution.”

Nature, 2025. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11203-1  (About DOIs).

#267. How long could HDDs and SSDs remain expensive?

If you've spent a considerable amount of time building and maintaining custom PCs, you've likely seen it all. You've seen fads come and go, and you've seen emerging technology become permanent fixtures. Recently, however, we've all seen the disastrous end results of what is now being referred to as RAMageddon.

The chip shortage that we're dealing with today often feels reminiscent of the one from 2020, when both video game consoles and prebuilt PCs became frustratingly difficult to obtain, though they each have different root causes. While RAM, processors and even video cards are experiencing some astonishingly high prices, two PC components that have found themselves slightly shielded from the massive price hikes are hard drives and solid-state drives.

Though they are still being heavily impacted, the industry appears to be heading toward some form of relief. It may just take a bit of time to get to the finish line.

The current market for HDDs and SSDs is an interesting one. Regardless of whether you're buying an enthusiast drive with upwards of 20 terabytes of storage or something on the lower end, you're going to be paying significantly higher prices due to the chip shortage.

In the long run, however, deciding on the actual purchase of any kind of storage is a complicated one. Traditional mechanical hard drives have been pushed aside for years in favor of SSDs, but they do still have their uses in today's market. Though they are not ideal for gaming and often seem to move at a snail's pace compared to even baseline-level SSDs, they do function quite well for mass storage of photos, videos and documents.

They also tend to be exceptionally well built, as companies have been making them for decades. Standard HDDs have a tendency to last for quite a long time, and to that end, the comparative price between them and more advanced SSDs is nothing but a good thing. Since SSDs use flash memory, which is undergoing its own shortage, a lot of NVMe and SATA SSDs are being hit somewhat harder.

The year 2027 has been earmarked as the first wave of relief from the higher prices. Though it's often described as just a slight decrease, any bit of money saved is worth it in the long run. Ultimately, the full weight of RAMageddon's first crushing blow looks like it will start winding down, and the far-reaching effects are something that we've dealt with for a while.

Heading into 2027, industry analysts have been quite clear that things will see a trend toward lower prices, but the global lows of pre-COVID times are likely a permanent thing of the past. Indeed, it's possible that many of us may not even notice the slight dip in prices, as something that is expensive being just slightly less expensive may not feel as warm and fuzzy as one may hope.

The general consensus about when HDD and SSD prices may drop isn't a very reassuring one. 2027 may see some subtle drops, but if you're looking to build a PC, or even upgrade a drive in your current setup, it's probably wise to wait until at least the end of 2027 or beyond. Most reports have indicated that 2029 or 2030 will be when prices start to see a sharper, more noticeable drop.

#266. How to use your phone's camera to translate anything

Our phones have the ability to make sense of other languages (and it requires minimal effort on our part).

If you're a frequent traveler, you may frequently encounter signage or other text in foreign languages. That's all well and good if you have enough knowledge to piece together a translation, but if you can't even understand the alphabet in question, you're faced with a much bigger challenge.

The good news is that your phone's camera can recognize and translate just about any text in seconds, even if the language uses an entirely different script. While a translation app may seem like the obvious choice for this task, it's actually not always your best bet. Depending on the languages involved and the context, you may sometimes need more than one tool. Luckily, your phone's camera is all you need to translate pretty much anything in the real world.

For over a decade now, the Google Translate app has offered a dedicated camera mode. Simply install the app from the Google Play Store on Android or the App Store on iOS, open it, and tap the Camera icon located at the bottom of your screen. This will open up a viewfinder, allowing you to point your phone's camera at anything in the real world.

You can select any two of Google Translate's hundreds of languages for the translation. The default "Detect language" option in the source field is handy if you've come across a language you cannot identify. The app translates text in real time, so you don't even need to capture an image. You may also want to download frequently-used languages within Google Translate. This allows you to translate text offline — handy if you're preparing for an upcoming trip.

You can also use Google Lens on Android, which many phones include out of the box these days. This eliminates the need for a dedicated translation app. On Google Pixel phones, Lens is available as a shortcut within the search bar on the home screen. Otherwise, you can find it as an icon in the app drawer. Recent iOS versions also have a translation feature baked into the camera app through the Live Text feature. To access it, open the Camera app on your iPhone and point the device at any text you come across. You should see a yellow frame appear around the text and a grid icon towards the bottom of the viewfinder. Tap this icon and select Translate.

While Google Translate has served me well, it can fall short of expectations. While traveling in Vietnam, for instance, I found that the app struggled to identify diacritics in printed text through my phone's camera. This was a major problem because a word can have two completely different meanings depending on whether the letters have the correct diacritics. In my experience, another area where Google Translate stumbles is restaurant menus. Menus often use informal shorthand or a single word, meaning the app may lack enough context for an accurate translation.

The solution I've found is to translate via an AI app. These apps often cannot translate in real time and require an internet connection, but I've found that the output quality is far and away better than Google Translate. Modern AI models understand context, so sending a picture of a menu will typically yield food-related translations. Even if your image is blurry or difficult to read, the AI model often understands the intended meaning based on the surrounding text instead of replying with gibberish.

You can use any AI app such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude. You'll need to upload a picture of the text you need translated and type a short instruction, such as "Translate to English," before sending the message. The AI will reply with the translated text, but cannot overlay the translation over your image as Google Translate does. The other downside to this method is that it's much more expensive — ChatGPT's free tier limits you to a few image uploads every day, and even then, processing can take a few seconds. Still, I often use it as a last resort whenever traditional translation methods fail me.

#264. Why it's important to never plug power strips into each other

Your power strip needs a wall outlet and not another power strip.

There are so many work-from-home devices nowadays that running a home office or a gaming area easily turns into a charging and power-consumption nightmare of tangled cords, ports and outlets. The idea of stringing power strips together by plugging one into the other (daisy-chaining) is a convenient, understandable solution. More outlets and ports mean more organization and power for each device. Unfortunately, it's not the greatest of ideas, especially if tripped breakers and house fires aren't on your to-do list.

The first problem is that adding sockets doesn't increase electrical capacity. Everything connected to the second strip draws electricity through the first strip's plug and internal components. The first strip is now carrying the combined load of the devices plugged into the second strip. The second problem is each strip's maximum rating, typically expressed in amps. If a second power strip is plugged into the first and the first is maxed out, the second strip could be the straw that breaks the proverbial camel's back, drawing too much and overheating the first strip.

Pushing too much current through the internal wiring and components of the first power strip generates "resistive heating." Given enough time, it can melt the casing and wire insulation, possibly igniting nearby materials. In the aforementioned home office scenario, flammable materials are abundantly present in most cases.

What to do when one power strip isn't enough depends on what you need. Do you need more sockets? Ports? More reach or more electrical capacity? Where low-power electronics are concerned, a single power strip that's more generous with its number of outlets is your best bet. Just make sure that the total load remains within the power strip's rating. A strip with 8 outlets doesn't necessarily supply more power than a strip with only 4 outlets. It's a separate consideration you have to be wary of.

If distance is the issue, find a strip with a longer cord. Don't reach for an extension cord as a matter of convenience. NFPA explicitly advises folks to avoid that arrangement, since extension cords have their own ratings and too many devices plugged in at once can exceed those ratings. Of course, you can do the math based on the cord's rating, the strip and everything plugged into it, but most people aren't aware of the limitations.

If a single strip is tripping the breaker, adding a new one and dispersing the devices won't solve the problem. In fact, treat it as a warning that requires your immediate attention. Never use a strip with damaged casings, scorch marks or loose connections. It's not something you can wrap in half a roll of electrical tape and call it a day.

As it happens, plugging a power strip into a power strip isn't the only thing you should avoid. High-power appliances can easily overload a power strip if it's not rated to handle it. Space heaters are a common one in this regard. They draw a fairly substantial amount of current and should only be plugged into a proper wall outlet. Microwaves and refrigerators are other prime examples.

For the safest route, use ordinary power strips with ordinary devices like PCs and printers, or to charge your phone. Also, six outlets doesn't mean it needs six devices plugged into it at once. Check the devices and match them against the power strip's ratings. They may seem like it, but power strips are not all-purpose devices for whatever needs power at the moment.

Lastly, a surge protector doesn't change the dynamics here. Surge protection deals with sudden voltage spikes but, like power strips, it won't magically conjure more energy capacity. Basic safety guidance for surge protectors also advises against daisy-chaining. The potential consequences warrant a repeat: check the surge protector's or power strip's rating and what you're plugging into it. If it's not enough, simply use another outlet or purchase a separate power strip and use another wall socket to run it.

#263. Googling "Zelda" today offers a glimpse of how search worked in 1998

The year was 1998. Britney Spears topped the charts, Bill Clinton was impeached, and a couple of little websites called Google and Ars Technica came online. It was also the year Nintendo released The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on the Nintendo 64. Google, which has come to dominate the Internet (Ars is still working on that), is celebrating the imminent release of the Ocarina of Time remaster by temporarily transporting us back to that storied year with a search Easter egg.

To access the Google time machine, you just have to search for either “Zelda” or “Ocarina of Time.” Google will load the standard 2026 results page, but you’ll see an animated Master Sword in the lower right corner. It appears on both mobile and desktop—just click the sword and enjoy the show.

After a little time-skipping animation and a Link shout (you know the one), you’ll swear it’s 1998 again. The search page is transformed into a simple list of blue links with retro Google branding. This is particularly apt given the time-shifting mechanics in Ocarina of Time.

Classic Google used to provide a list of 10 links on each page, but there are only seven included in the Easter egg. This is a curated list of links rather than a real search. You get the official Nintendo Zelda page, Zelda on Wikipedia, Zelda games on Amazon, and a couple more.

You can go back to the modern version of Google’s search results at any time by clicking the sword again. Oh, you don’t want to do that? Sadly, this is a very limited experience. The Google of today is much different, and if you try to search for anything from the retro interface, you are immediately booted back to 2026 with all the AI, sponsored content, suggested searches, and social media links.

The Ocarina of Time left its mark on a generation of gamers, and clearly, some of them went on to work at Google. The company’s intention is probably to leverage nostalgia to build hype for Nintendo’s big launch, but there’s also something a little sad about this. Google’s push into generative AI is transforming search in a way that many people don’t like. Seeing the simple, minimalist roots of Google search on display drives home how much the company’s core product has changed.

The Ocarina of Time has changed a lot, too. The remastered game has been completely re-created, with slick Switch 2 graphics, modern controls for movement and camera, numerous quality-of-life improvements, and more. The game is available for preorder now at $60 for digital and $70 for physical. It launches on November 5 for Nintendo Switch 2.

#262. The reason why some iPhone calls don't have a decline option, and others do

Your iPhone's incoming call screen isn't as mysterious as it seems.

At some point, everyone's been burned by their iPhone going off in the worst possible place. When you see there's no option to decline the call, it's a mad scramble to press every side button or sling the phone through a wall at the speed of sound. But you've seen the on-screen option to decline calls before, so what gives? Fair warning: it's a really simple, forehead-slapping answer. When your iPhone is locked, incoming calls display the "slide to answer" control. When your iPhone is unlocked, you get the option to answer or decline the call.

Depending on your Incoming Calls setting, Accept and Decline buttons appear in a compact banner or across the entire screen, but both options remain. No, you didn't disable anything by accident. This is simply how the iPhone operates by default, right out of the box. On the bright side, it's not set in stone; you can make adjustments via Settings.

You don't need an on-screen button to decline or silence a call, however. You can press the side button twice quickly to decline and send the caller straight to voicemail. Or, you can press either volume button to silence the ring without declining the call. You can do this whether the iPhone screen is locked or not.

The person calling will probably know their call was just rejected if you hit the side button twice the moment your iPhone starts ringing. The practical effect is pretty obvious. Fortunately, rejecting a phone call doesn't have to come off as rude, because you can let the caller know why you rejected it. An iPhone's incoming call interface includes a Message option that lets you send a text instead of answering. There are a few useful prepared options, as well as a custom alternative if you prefer.

If the incoming call pops up as a banner while you're busy, tap the banner to reveal more options, then select Message. Go with a prepared reply or quickly fire off a text by choosing Custom. Now you can provide some context to the caller and explain why they're being sent straight to voicemail.

You can also change the prepared replies well in advance. Open Settings > Apps > Phone > Respond with Text, then select a response and edit it accordingly. For instance, "I'm working right now" and "Please text me; I'm busy" both speak volumes in a few short words. It's a nifty little feature and only takes a few minutes to set up.

Despite the 1991 Telephone Consumer Protection Act, telemarketers, spam and robocalls are something we all deal with on a regular basis. According to the Federal Trade Commission, there were more than 2.6 million Do Not Call complaints in fiscal year 2025. Some callers are more persistent than others, and even if you block one number, they'll call back from another slightly different number. But it's worth the effort to block them all. Find the number you just rejected in Recents, tap it (or the Info button in Classic view), scroll to the bottom of the screen, select Block Caller and confirm.

You can use a broader setting to screen unknown callers as well. Go to Settings > Apps > Phone > Screen Unknown Callers (iOS 26 and later). From here, you can select Never, Ask Reason for Calling or Silence. Consider the middle option, just in case the unknown number is someone you know and the call is important.

But if you choose Silence, every unknown call will go straight to voicemail without ringing. Just remember that life comes at you fast, and that unknown number may be someone you recently met or someone who lost their phone and really needs to contact you. Convenience always comes with a caveat or two.

#260. What pet cemeteries reveal about being human

Editor’s Note:  Eric Tourigny is a lecturer in historical archaeology at Newcastle University, UK. His research interprets osteological and material culture remains alongside historic texts to examine changing human-animal relationships in Europe and North America over the past 500 years. The views expressed in this commentary are his own. Read more opinion on CNN.

Why do we bury our departed loved ones in a cemetery? A primary purpose is to provide survivors with an opportunity to grieve and gain a sense of closure. The cemetery is a place for the living as much as it is a place for the dead.

But what about when the dearly departed are not human – but our pets?

The Spanish city of Barcelona recently announced that it will be investing in the establishment of the country’s first public pet cemetery. Set to open next year, it will offer both burials and cremations – with an estimated 7,000 carried out each year.

For me, as someone who has spent years researching the development of pet cemeteries elsewhere in the world, this news came as a shock. Barcelona is a densely populated city with limited privately owned land – one where 50% of families own a pet.

How did a city that is home to 180,000 dogs not already have a public pet cemetery? Until now, the service was only provided by the private sector, according to Barcelona’s Councilor for Climate Emergency and Ecological Transition, Eloi Badia. He added that the municipal-funded initiative was sparked by “constant public demand.”

After all, public pet cemeteries have been around in Europe and the Americas since the late 19th century. Britain’s first public pet cemetery appeared in London’s Hyde Park in 1881. New York’s Hartsdale pet cemetery was founded in 1896, followed a few years later by Paris’ ornate Cimetière des Chiens in 1899.

I became interested in the history of modern pet burial practices while investigating the archaeological record of a centuries-old house in Toronto. I came across a (very) large dog buried in the back garden which, according to the historical record, was occupied between 1840 and 1870.

This dog survived to an elderly age but, sadly, suffered from degenerative joint disease and severe infections during his last months. His ailments progressed to such a state that suggest he received some level of care in his final weeks. He then was buried in a personal plot behind the family home.

This elderly dog led me to think about the different ways people interact with the bodies of their pets after death. Could this behavior be reflective of the relationships they held with their animals in life? In this instance, why take the time to carefully bury a dog in its own space when other, arguably easier options existed?

This, after all, was an era when people often disposed of their dead pets in the river, or might have sold their bodies for meat and skin.

Good hygiene is an obvious reason to choose a burial – no one wants decomposing animal bodies in the street or their garden – but that wouldn’t immediately warrant a personalized, dedicated burial and gravestone.

The most straight forward option would be to dispose of a deceased animal with the household waste. But such treatment would evidently feel less ceremonious and would not offer appropriate emotional closure to what was likely an important relationship.

Like the burial of people, the burial of pets is an intimate cultural practice, one that changes over time and is reflective of the changing relationships that a society has with its cherished creatures.

My study of historic gravestones and epitaphs in Britain from the Victorian period to today shows this changing human-animal relationship. In the 19th century, gravestones were often dedicated to a “loving friend” or “devoted companion,” suggesting pets were mostly considered important friends.

By the early 20th century, pets had become members of the family – evidenced by the appearance of family surnames on the gravestones, and loving epitaphs written by “Mummy and Daddy.”

By the early 20th century, pets had become members of the family – evidenced by the appearance of family surnames on the gravestones, and loving epitaphs written by “Mummy and Daddy.”

Society’s changing attitude towards the role of animals in the afterlife can also be found. Fast-forward a few decades later, and gravestones were more likely to reference a reunion then earlier ones. For example, the owners of Denny, the “brave little cat” buried in an east London cemetery in 1952, wrote on his epitaph “God bless until we meet again.”

I wonder what the epitaphs in Barcelona’s new cemetery will reveal about modern Catalan relationships with animals.

Over time, our ways of treating our animal dead appear to reflect an even closer relationship in life. Once strictly forbidden by law, the last decade saw many jurisdictions, like the state of New York, allowing the co-burial of cremated animals and people, which will undoubtedly lead to changing funerary and commemoration practices for both humans and animals.

For me, the most remarkable similarity between modern and historic pet cemeteries is the striking evidence for the heartbreak and taboos around grieving for animals.

The connection that someone has with their pet can be just as strong and just as significant as their relationships with other humans. Yet today, as in over 100 years ago, individuals continue to struggle to find the appropriate outlet to express their pain, hiding heartache for fear of the social repercussions that might come with public acknowledgment of the existence of such a bond.

The RSPCA reassures the public on its website that they should not feel shame for their grief. In the UK, charities like the Blue Cross and Rainbow Bridge Pet Loss Grief Center offer counseling to bereaved humans.

Close relationships between people and animals have existed for millennia, but in western European cultures, there were few acceptable ways to mourn that relationship. As society becomes more accepting of the importance of human-animal relationships to our collective wellbeing, it is not surprising to see us follow rituals resembling those we use to mourn the loss of our closest human relationships.

At an estimated cost of €200 ($217) per service at the new Barcelona cemetery, it is important to acknowledge that this opportunity to grieve will not be financially available to everyone in the city.

This will not be a space for all of the city’s pets. Pet owners may opt to keep cremated remains within their home or spread out ashes in a meaningful location instead. Online forums and digital pet cemeteries also provide other opportunities to commemorate the relationship and express grief.

Whether one chooses a pet cemetery or not, there are many acceptable ways to express your grief – and to remember your relationship with the important animals in your life.

#257. Third person dies of bird flu since virus started jumping to livestock

The threat is still considered to be low, but the virus continues to spread.

A person in Washington state has died from bird flu after exposure at an infected dairy farm, state health officials reported Sunday. It marks the third human bird flu death in the US since a strain of highly pathogenic (H5) avian influenza (HPAI) made the unprecedented jump from wild, migratory birds to dairy cows, which was first reported in the US in March 2024.

“Our hearts go out to the individual’s family and loved ones during this difficult time,” Dave Atteberry, health officer for the Yakima Health District, said in a statement. “Avian influenza can cause severe illness, particularly among people who have underlying health conditions. While this is a serious and heartbreaking outcome, the risk to the general public remains low.”

In all, three people have tested positive for bird flu in Washington since the virus was reported in dairy cattle in the state on October 8. All three have been in Yakima County. While announcing the death on Sunday, officials also reported the third case. That case, like the first case, was in a person who had exposure to an infected dairy herd in the county. Both people have reportedly not experienced severe illness nor been hospitalized.

Since the October 8 report of infected herds, Washington state has had 40 detections of bird flu in dairy cows, according to the US Department of Agriculture. Most of those have been in Yakima County, which has reported detections in 33 herds.

This year, the USDA has reported 134 cases of bird flu in cattle, including cases in Texas, Washington, Idaho, Utah, and Kansas. The USDA lists no other reports of cases in other domestic livestock, including swine. But the virus has continued to spread in other wild and captive mammals. A report last month from ProPublica revealed that the virus is raging on a mink farm in Utah. The report raised alarm because mink is a species that could give the virus opportunities to mutate to better spread among humans.

To date, no human-to-human transmission of HPAI has been reported from the over 70 human cases detected since 2024. Of the cases, only three have resulted in death. The first death was in a 65-year-old Louisiana resident with underlying health conditions, who became critically ill in January 2025 after exposure to infected wild and backyard birds. The second death, in November 2025, was reported by Washington state officials as an older adult with underlying health conditions who also had exposure to infected backyard birds.

In 2017, major CEOs from across the country came together to oppose North Carolina’s transgender bathroom law. In 2019, they called abortion bans “bad for business.”

After the deadly attack on the US Capitol on January 6, 2021, many of corporate America’s biggest names denounced the rioters and pledged to halt their political giving.

Recently, more than 1,000 companies promised to voluntarily curtail their operations in Russia in protest of Moscow’s war on Ukraine.

Dick’s Sporting Goods stopped selling semi-automatic, assault-style rifles at stores and Citigroup put new restrictions on gun sales by business customers after the mass shooting at a high school in Parkland, Florida, in 2018.

A year later, after mass shootings at a Walmart in El Paso, Texas, and a nightclub in Dayton, Ohio, Walmart ended handgun ammunition sales.

Corporate leadership has long been vocal on the issue of gun control – in 2019 and again this past summer nearly 150 major companies – including Lululemon, Lyft, Bain Capital, Bloomberg LP, Permanente Medical Group and Unilever – called gun violence a “public health crisis” and demanded that the US Senate pass legislation to address it.

That’s why corporate America’s silence in the wake of the latest mass shooting at a school in Nashville is so jarring. The United States has come to rely on the increasing power of large corporations as political advocates.

But Yale professor Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, a vocal advocate of corporate social responsibility who has a direct line to major CEOs around the globe, said that top executives are forlorn. Their previous efforts haven’t done much to push the needle on gun control legislation and without more backing, they don’t know what else they can do at the moment, he said.

Before the Bell spoke with Sonnenfeld, who runs Yale School of Management’s Chief Executive Leadership Institute, a nonprofit educational and research institute focused on CEO leadership and corporate governance.

This interview has been edited for clarity and length.

Before the Bell: CEOs have been quiet about gun reform since the latest mass school shooting in Nashville, have you heard anything about plans to speak out?

Jeffrey Sonnenfeld: Where is everybody else? Where is all of civil society? CEOs are just one group of people and it’s like we’re turning to them to be our saviors on every topic. They’ve joined causes with valor and nobility but they can’t just be taking cause after cause as if there’s nobody else in society. The social change that happened in the 1960s wasn’t being led primarily by CEOs. Social changes really happened when we saw the interfaith activity of clergy locking arms and canvassing legislators. We saw campuses alive and aroused. Where’s all the student activism?

The CEOs are still the most active even if they’re less active than they were six months ago. They’re not there as hired hands of shareholders to fill the role of politicians and civic leaders. They’re there to join that chorus, but they don’t want to be the only one singing.

So is this what you’re hearing from top CEOs? Have they gotten tired of advocating?

I just got off of a CEO call on voting rights and this morning we had a forum on sustainability – CEOs are still the most active on these fronts. It’s the same thing on immigration reform. If a CEO was working an 18 hour day on a 12 day week, they still couldn’t address all of the issues that need addressing.

The nation’s CEOs are waiting for everybody else to join them. They don’t need to restate something they’ve already stated. They’ve jumped in the pool, where’s everybody else?

So what do you think has led to this complacency amongst Americans and the growing reliance on CEOs to advocate on our behalf?

They’ve taken a very strong stance and they’ve gone out further than the general public. They are where the general public is on surveys, but they’re not where the general public is on action in the streets. So we’re ready for others to now do something. Enough already on saying ‘what are the CEOs doing?’ Social capital is as valuable as financial capital. CEOs understand that in their soul, they want there to be social capital. They want there to be public trust, but they need the rest of civil society to join them. And that’s their frustration.

But don’t these CEOs hold the purse strings in terms of donating to powerful politicians?

You would think that, but since the 2020 elections much less of campaign contributions have come from big business. Since the 2021 run on the Capitol, a lot of businesses either had an official moratorium or they’ve given mere pennies to politicians. The common impression on the street that CEOs are controlling campaign purses strings is 100% wrong.

Tesla reported. a modest 4% rise in sales in the first quarter compared to the final three months of last year, despite a series of price cuts on its lower priced vehicles and talk by CEO Elon Musk about strong demand at those lower prices.

The first quarter also marked the fourth straight quarter that Tesla has produced more vehicles than it has delivered to customers. Some of that may be due to the ramp up in production at two new factories, one in Texas, the other in Germany, which opened last spring, and a lag between that increased production and sales.

Tesla said there was an increase in the number of its more expensive models, the Model S and Model X, in transit to Europe, the Middle East and Africa, as well as to the Asia Pacific region.

But it does mean that over the last 12 months Tesla has produced 78,000 more cars than it has sold, suggesting that talk of strong demand by Tesla executives may not be backed up by the numbers.

“Early this year, we had a price adjustment. After that, we actually generated a huge demand, more than we can produce, really,” said Tom Zhu, Tesla’s executive in charge of global production and sales. “And as Elon said, as long as you offer a product with value at affordable price, you don’t have to worry about demand.”

#254. How Iliana Yotova won the presidential election in Bulgaria

Iliana Yotova won the presidential election in Bulgaria, promising to be a "president of peace." But the campaign showed how divided Bulgarians are about the war in Ukraine and drone attacks in the Black Sea.

"We are choosing between war and peace," Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev told voters ahead of Sunday's presidential election runoff between incumbent President Iliana Yotova, who opposes military aid to Ukraine and favors dialogue with Russia, and former caretaker Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov, who is regarded as staunchly pro-European and pro-Ukrainian.

With these words, it was clear that Sunday's runoff had turned into a kind of referendum on the country's foreign policy and stance on the war in Ukraine.

Now that the official results are in and it is clear that Iliana Yotova won the election decisively by 57.6% to Gyurov's 39.5%, Radev claims that Bulgarians have chosen peace.

When the presidential election campaign began in Bulgaria on September 25, there did not seem to be any doubt about the outcome: Iliana Yotova was well ahead in the polls on 44.5%. Gyurov, her main rival, trailed far behind on 26.1%.

Yotova was backed by both the prime minister and his ruling Progressive Bulgaria party, which won an absolute majority in the parliamentary election on April 19.

But the first round turned out to be much tighter than anticipated.

While Yotova got 34.8% of the vote in the first round, Gyurov was close behind on 31.95%, which meant that a runoff between the two was necessary.

While Yotova won the runoff convincingly, both the campaign and the outcome showed that the Bulgarian electorate is divided.

This division is both generational and geographical, explains Dimitar Ganev, sociologist and political scientist at the Trend market and electoral research agency.

"Younger voters — those aged between 18 and 40 — favor Gyurov. Those over 40 tend to prefer Yotova," Ganev told DW. "It also appears that Gyurov dominates in the capital, Sofia. In smaller regional cities, other towns and villages, Yotova dominates decisively," he said.

This divide was also evident during the campaign.

While Andrey Gyurov relied mainly on social media for his campaign, Yotova chose to speak mostly to supporters of Progressive Bulgaria in closed venues.

At such events, the war in Ukraine was always high on the agenda.

"As long as I am president, and if you place your trust in me, not a single Bulgarian soldier will go to Ukraine," Yotova declared at an election rally on October 6 — even though according to the Bulgarian Constitution, only parliament (not the president) has the authority to send troops abroad or declare war.

Throughout the campaign, she referred to her opponents as "warmongers" and described herself as the "president of peace."

"We won because we talked to people about income and about peace," Yotova said after the election.

In this, she is similar to Prime Minister Rumen Radev.

When it comes to Ukraine, Radev regularly speaks of the need for peace and avoids calling Russia an "aggressor." Both Radev and Yotova oppose military aid to Ukraine and criticize European leaders for not making sufficient efforts to engage with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Gyurov, on the other hand, has sharply criticized Russian aggression in Ukraine.

Appointed caretaker prime minister by Yotova in February, Gyurov in March signed a security cooperation agreement with Ukraine, provoking the disapproval of both Yotova and Radev.

In the weeks leading up to the election, several ships in the Black Sea were hit by drones off the Bulgarian coast.

The European Council criticized Russia for the escalation, and the European Parliament called on the EU and its member states "to consider deploying an EU naval operation" there.

Prime Minister Radev, however, was not as equivocal, going no further than summoning the Russian ambassador and stating that "logic suggests that the outcome" of the attacks in the Black Sea "is to the advantage of the Russian Federation."

Just days before the runoff, he noted that "two ships were struck and sunk in Romanian territorial waters" after Romania had held Russia responsible for the attacks in the Black Sea.

"Many people think that once the aggressor is identified, the attacks will stop," he said, downplaying the Kremlin's responsibility. His remarks drew criticism from politicians and the media in Romania.

Yotova also did not name Russia as the perpetrator, instead saying during her campaign that she did not want to see "foreign flags in Bulgaria" — a clear reference to the Ukrainian flag, which has been displayed outside several institutions in Bulgaria as a sign of solidarity with the war-torn country.

Most opposition parties, including the right-wing conservative GERB led by former long-serving Prime Minister Boyko Borisov, refused to field a candidate for the presidency, which is one reason why turnout on Sunday was less than 30%.

In the first round, the pro-Russian candidate Kostadin Kostadinov from the nationalist Vazrazhdane (Revival) party came third with 12.5% of the vote. According to Dimitar Ganev, around 70% of Vazrazhdane voters backed Yotova in the runoff.

To secure their support, Yotova targeted pro-Russian voters.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"Russia is by no means an enemy of Bulgaria," she said in a podcast interview just two days before the runoff, adding "Russia is part of our history, and I very much hope that it will be a key factor in the future security architecture across Europe, including for us."

In the days leading up to the vote, some of her supporters began claiming that the opposition was preparing a "Maidan," a reference to the Ukrainian revolution of 2014 that culminated in the ousting of President Viktor Yanukkovych, who had close ties to Moscow.

"All of Gyurov's lackeys are speaking openly about inevitable protests. They're using prime time to stir up a Maidan. Every single one of them," Sonya Momchilova, who was appointed to the media regulator by Radev, wrote on Facebook on Sunday.

Similar claims were made by both former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban and former Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic ahead of this year's elections in their countries.

"This claim that Ms. Yotova will be a president of peace is directly linked to the incitement of a fear of war," said former Defense Minister Todor Tagarev, who was part of the committee that nominated Andrey Gyurov for president. "Bulgaria will be in a much worse position within Europe and NATO under her leadership," he said during a TV interview.

Dimitar Ganev, on the other hand, sees no threat to Bulgaria's commitment to the EU and NATO. "Over two-thirds of Bulgarians do not question the country's geopolitical orientation, and around two-thirds have a positive attitude towards the EU," he told DW.

But the positions of Radev and Yotova, which many view as ambivalent, mobilized both the pro-European camp and Eurosceptic voters, who, according to Ganev, make up around a third of the country's population.

According to Prime Minister Rumen Radev and President Iliana Yotova, the Bulgarian people chose peace in the presidential election. Nevertheless, the war continues.

#253. A fresh wave of cyberattacks has hit Europe’s supermarket refrigerators, destroying food across countries

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE.

A second wave of cyberattacks is suspected to have hit supermarket refrigerators across Europe, causing fridges to increase temperatures and spoil food at dozens of stores across Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg, and Sweden.

Supermarket giants Ahold Delhaize and Colruyt confirmed the hacks overnight, with one Belgian company that operates Delhaize’s systems saying that the hackers had changed the settings to defrost, per Reuters. Stores have experienced heavy food losses from the cyberattacks, forcing supermarkets to throw out goods that had defrosted or were otherwise no longer consumable.

The cyberattacks follow earlier refrigerator hacks in France last month that caused food spoilage at hundreds of supermarkets by deliberately raising the temperature on the units. Security researchers said that the cause of the hacks was internet-connected refrigerators made by Danish company Danfoss, which was no longer providing security updates. Security company Claroty warned back in August that those refrigerator units were at risk of remote hacks and outages.

The freezer hacks underscore how cyberattacks can have real-world effects, including on the food supply chain, often as a result of weak or overlooked cybersecurity practices. In 2025, a cyberattack on food distributor giant UNFI resulted in food shortages and empty shelves at grocery stores and supermarkets across the United States.

U.S. Department of Defense officials are reportedly investigating whether freezer units on military bases were hacked by Iran-backed hackers. Iranian hackers were also blamed for cyberattacks targeting U.S. water providers earlier this year.

#250. Ninja’s first-ever microwave just replaced two of my kitchen appliances at once

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE.

I never thought I’d get excited about replacing my microwave, but the Ninja Crispi Microwave and Air Fryer has made a pretty convincing case for ditching two appliances and making room for one. Combining a microwave with a built-in air fryer, it’s designed to speed up everyday cooking, give leftovers their crunch back and, perhaps best of all, free up some valuable kitchen counter space.

Priced at $449.99, it’s certainly not a budget-friendly microwave. But this is no ordinary machine for heating leftover soup. Ninja has paired a 1,000W microwave with a 1,700W air fryer system, powered by its FusionCrisp technology, which combines the speed of microwave cooking with the golden, crispy results you’d typically expect from an air fryer.

Think leftover pizza, chicken tenders, fries, and all those foods that tend to turn sad and soggy in a traditional microwave. Instead, the idea is to get food that’s piping hot and juicy on the inside, with a deliciously crisp, golden finish on the outside. In other words, no more choosing between speed and texture.

Of course, microwave and air fryer combinations aren’t entirely new. Brands such as Smeg have already explored the concept, while plenty of modern microwaves come with a range of additional cooking functions.

What makes the Ninja Crispi Microwave particularly interesting, however, is its FusionCrisp technology, which is designed to bring both cooking methods together rather than simply offering two separate functions. It comes with a 5.5-quart glass cooking dish and a nonstick crisper plate, which sits on top when you want to air fry and crisp up your food.

Another part that makes it stand out is that there isn’t a rotating plate inside, opening up a lot more space to cook more dishes at once.

It’s not just about reheating leftovers. For example, if you want to make a pasta bake, the microwave can cook the pasta, while the air fryer crisps up the cheese on top.

There’s one thing to consider before buying it, though. Measuring 20.3 x 17.56 x 14.1 inches, the microwave is hardly compact. It takes up a fair amount of counter space, so while it could free up room if you’re replacing a separate microwave and air fryer, it’s not necessarily the ideal solution for a small apartment kitchen.

Then there’s the $449.99 price tag. That’s a considerable amount to spend on a microwave, particularly when a basic model can handle everyday reheating for a fraction of the cost. But if you’re someone who regularly reaches for both a microwave and an air fryer, the combination could make a lot more sense.
